articles.title: US bans vehicles from China’s BYD at Japan military base, calling them ‘unacceptable’ risk
articles.summary:
US military says the restrictions on the electric vehicles at Kadena airbase also apply to delivery drivers and taxis

One of America’s biggest overseas military bases has banned vehicles…

blocks.text: One of America’s biggest overseas military bases has banned vehicles made by the Chinese electric vehicle maker BYD over security concerns, the US military in Japan said on Tuesday.

The ban, which went into effect this week at Kadena airbase on the southern Japanese island of Okinawa, has fueled speculation that similar measures could be taken at other US military facilities as part of Washington’s crackdown on Chinese technology it suspects of being used to collect sensitive information.
“These vehicles present an unacceptable and unmitigable risk to our personnel and our mission,” Lieut Col Alli Stormer, a spokesperson for the US air force 18th Wing at Kadena, said in a statement.

The restrictions apply to all BYD vehicles, including privately owned cars, taxis and delivery vehicles, reports said, adding that security personnel stationed at the base’s gates had been instructed to block BYD vehicles and instruct drivers to turn around.
Kadena, the biggest US air force base east Asia, would be directly involved in responding to a crisis involving China, Russia or North Korea.

Its inventory includes the powerful Typhon missile system, which is said to be capable of firing Tomahawk missiles as far as 1,600km, putting parts of China and Russia within striking distance. Kadena also hosts fighter planes and aircraft used for mid-air refuelling, surveillance and reconnaissance, according to its website.

blocks.caption: A US military plane takes off at Kadena air force base on Japan’s southern island of Okinawa. Photograph: Issei Kato/Reuters

blocks.text: The move comes amid concerns of potential information leaks via vehicle-mounted technologies such as cameras, sensors and GPS devices, South Korea’s Yonhap news agency said.

American military officials have not identified a specific threat, but the ban is part of wider measures taken by the US and other western countries to restrict Chinese smart technology in vehicles, mobile phones and other devices they fear could be used to “spy” on their owners.

In June the Pentagon added BYD to a list of 188 Chinese firms it believes have ties to the country’s military, drawing a protest from Beijing. The blacklist also includes the automaker Nio, e-commerce firm Alibaba and internet company Baidu.
The US defence department banned the sale and use of smartphones from Chinese companies Huawei and ZTE at military bases worldwide in 2018, again citing security concerns.

China has imposed similar restrictions on US-made Tesla vehicles. In 2021, it barred them from some government compounds due to security concerns over ⁠cameras installed on the vehicles. Beijing removed that restriction in 2024 after Tesla won an endorsement from the country’s top auto industry association.
BYD, which has not immediately responded publicly to the Kadena ban, overtook Tesla as the world’s biggest seller of battery-electric vehicles in 2025.

It is now expanding overseas, including in the world’s fourth-biggest auto market, Japan, where in July it launched its Racco electric minicar in the hope that the small, cost-efficient vehicle would carve out a place in a market dominated by domestic brands.
With Reuters

articles.title: Ban or tiered limits? Meta, gov’t agencies discuss child online safety as Congress eyes social media ban
articles.summary: CICC says child safety ‘cannot be matched by promises alone,’ urging platforms to deliver results on safeguards for minors online

items: Meta hosted a forum in Manila to discuss children's online safety amid legislative efforts to restrict minors' access to social media.
The forum emphasized the need for effective safety measures and parental involvement, with discussions on the potential impact of a proposed ban on minors using social media.
Panelists advocated for a tiered approach to online access based on age, highlighting the importance of parental engagement and understanding in ensuring children's safety online.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – As Congress moves to reconcile legislation prohibiting minors from accessing social media and other high-risk digital services, Meta, the company behind Facebook and Instagram, hosted a forum to discuss children’s online safety on Monday, October 26, at the Ayala Malls Glorietta Activity Center.

Meta, together with the Department of Information and Communications Technology-Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (DICT-CICC), Department of Education (DepEd), National Youth Commission (NYC), and other stakeholders, hosted the forum to kick off the Digital Dialogue In Real Life, a free interactive exhibition that aims to take a comprehensive approach to youth digital well-being in the Philippines. The exhibit will run from Monday, October 26 to Friday, October 30.

The forum covered what platforms and families can do, from parental controls to conversations at home. This comes after incidents of school violence were reported nationwide, with investigators examining possible online influences, and as lawmakers weigh bills restricting minors’ access to social media.
During Meta’s event, DICT-CICC Director IV Noel Carlo Gracilla said that “children’s safety cannot be matched by promises alone.”

“Although we have secured [the platforms’] commitments, the CICC is not yet satisfied…. What we need to see is their action and effective solutions that will leave good results for our young people,” Gracilla said in his welcome message, speaking in Filipino.

He did, however, credit Meta’s quick responses to CICC requests with helping curb young people’s exposure to inappropriate content. He said the agency met in recent months with Discord, Reddit, Meta, and Roblox to raise concerns about their in-app safety features, especially for content unsuitable for minors.

At least eight incidents of school violence in the Philippines have been reported in 2026, including three deadly school shootings. Such incidents have prompted authorities to seek commitments from social media platforms.

blocks.caption: What school shootings in PH have in common

blocks.text: In August, after the second deadly shooting took place in Zamboanga City, the DICT said Meta and Roblox had agreed to enhance child-safety protections for users in the Philippines, including age verification and parental controls.

Senator Risa Hontiveros also said in the same month that the Philippine government had secured a commitment from Meta to provide user data to law enforcement when there is an imminent threat of violence.
Meta kicked off the exhibit with a forum to explore practical ways to address the risks children face online today. Among the panelists were:

items: Gio Tingson, head of public policy, Meta Philippines
Joseph Francisco Ortega, chairperson, NYC
Razzel Requesto, director IV, DepEd
Ysrael Diloy, child protection specialist, Stairway Foundation
Niel Steve Kintanar, external relations officer, Psychological Association of the Philippines
Mariel Kliatchko, influencer mom and school owner

blocks.text: The forum took place as Congress weighs whether to ban children from social media altogether. Under the Senate-approved Safe Media Access and Responsible Technology for Kids in Digital Spaces (SMART KIDS) bill, social media accounts determined as being owned or used by a minor will be suspended, restricted, disabled, or removed. It will also prevent users below 18 years old from creating accounts.
Diloy argued that a ban would push children out of online spaces where they have rights to expression and information.

“The rights holders are the children. The duty bearers are us, the adults. It’s our obligation to ensure the safety of the spaces the children move in, and to ensure that the children reap the benefits of technology,” Diloy said in Filipino.
“What we’re hoping for is for tech platforms to have accountability and responsibility,” Diloy said, adding that Meta’s launch of Teen Accounts with parental supervision tools is a welcome step.

blocks.caption: Why Congress should think twice about banning under-18s from social media

blocks.text: Meta’s Digital Dialogue IRL builds on its Screen Smart Philippines initiative, launched in June, which educates parents and teens about the safety features built into Teen Accounts across its products: Instagram, Facebook, Messenger, and Threads.

The protections in Teen Accounts include default private accounts, messaging restrictions, sensitive content limits, daily 60-minute time limit reminders, and a “sleep mode” that mutes notifications between 10 pm and 7 am. Teens cannot opt out or loosen these settings without a parent’s permission.
“Learning from other jurisdictions, without naming any country, we saw that bans are ineffective,” Tingson told Rappler on the sidelines of the event, saying that their solution is a tiered approach.

He argued that giving a five-year-old and an 18-year-old the same restrictions online would not address the core problem. “Their dimension of learning, of exploration, of responsibility is very different, so you want to make sure that the experience is appropriate. Because if we push people outside of the platform by doing bans, it’s either they circumvent it, or they delay learning,” he said.
Early evidence from Australia’s restrictions on social media for children under 16 years old found that roughly eight in ten children continued using social media despite the ban.
Hontiveros, the only senator to vote against the SMART KIDS bill, also earlier suggested a tiered access by age instead of a blanket ban.

blocks.caption: FAST FACTS: What changed in final version of the under-18 social media ban bill?

blocks.text: But whatever safety features social media platforms roll out only matter if families use them. Tingson told Rappler on the sidelines of the event that they’re still working on getting people to sign up for the Teen Accounts, saying: “We really need help in pushing for awareness in people enrolling.”
For the other members of the panel, using the features starts with a conversation between parent and child.
“Connection before correction. We can correct, we can punish. We can do all that. But do we understand [why we’re doing it]?” Kliatchko said in a mix of English and Filipino.

The influencer mom said that parents should protect, but it should be done with preparation. “You cannot just forbid your children to play Minecraft or Roblox…. You have to understand it. You have to be able to explain why [you’re setting boundaries],” she said.

Others on the panel echoed her. Kintanar said research shows relationships matter for mental health and well-being, while Ortega said parents can’t set limits for children they haven’t connected with.

blocks.caption: Preventing school violence starts at home, but gov’t must step up

blocks.text: The panel’s advice puts parents at the center. But what happens when even engaged parents become inundated with the apps’ features that are alleged to be built to hold teens’ attention?

blocks.caption: [DECODED] Child safety isn’t a parenting problem. It’s a platform failure.

blocks.text: Earlier this year, documents, primarily internal communications at the social media companies, were unsealed and shown in a Los Angeles trial brought by a young woman who said Instagram and YouTube fueled her addiction and depression. In March, the jury found Meta and YouTube liable for negligently designing products that harmed her. Meta has since appealed.

In August, a separate federal trial began on claims by 29 different US states. All 29 accused Meta of improperly collecting children’s data, and four lead states also alleged it deliberately designed Facebook and Instagram to hook children and misled the public about their safety.

Meta denied the claims and said it has strong protections for teenagers. About a week in, a federal judge approved an $18-billion settlement. Meta agreed without admitting wrongdoing, so the court made no finding on the states’ claims. – Rappler.com

articles.title: If convicted in impeachment trial, who will succeed Sara Duterte?
articles.summary: A political science professor says the choice of a successor will involve more than simply filling a vacancy

blocks.text: VEEP. Vice President Sara Duterte waves to supporters as she arrives at the Quezon City Regional Trial Court for the arraignment of her grave threats case, on October 9, 2026.
Noel Celis/Reuters
A political science professor says the choice of a successor will involve more than simply filling a vacancy
Even before Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial reaches a verdict, the question of who could replace her is already stirring debates among senator-judges.

Under the Constitution, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has the authority to nominate Duterte’s possible successor from among the sitting lawmakers but the decision will still be subject to congressional confirmation.

Article VII, Section 9 of the 1987 Constitution states: “Whenever there is a vacancy in the Office of the Vice President during the term for which he was elected, the President shall nominate a Vice-President from among the Members of the Senate and the House of Representatives who shall assume office upon confirmation by a majority vote of all the Members of both Houses of the Congress, voting separately.”

Over the weekend, Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero explained that while Marcos has the authority to nominate Duterte’s possible successor, the nominee must also meet the constitutional qualifications for vice president, including the age requirement.
This narrows the pool of potential nominees to sitting members of Congress who meet the constitutional requirements, including Escudero himself.
“I have yet to receive offers but as I’ve said before, I would not accept it because of a simple reason: conflict of interest,” Escudero said in his podcast.
“We tried her case so personally, I don’t think accepting that would be proper,” he added.

Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano lauded Escudero and urged other senator-judges to issue similar commitment to decline such proposals, citing the need to maintain political neutrality in the trial.

“It’s essential that in all impeachment proceedings, senator-judges are politically neutral and will have no incentive to convict except for evidence that proves the article/s of impeachment,” he said.
Cayetano’s remarks, however, did not sit well with Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson, who cautioned against preempting the decisions of other senator-judges.

“He should not preempt the decision of other senator-judges. Selecting the successor is under the prerogative of the President but of course, subject to the confirmation of the Congress,” Lacson said, adding he would decline if he would be offered such position.
“But I think [Cayetano’s statement] is uncalled for,” the senator added.

So what would Marcos look for in a successor? For political science professor Jean Franco of the University of the Philippines Diliman, the choice of a successor would involve more than simply filling a vacancy.
The President would have to consider the political implications of his nominee and whether that person could be trusted to assume the country’s highest office if necessary.
Franco identified several qualities Marcos might look for in a potential successor:

items: Someone who can help elevate public trust in the administration
Someone who can tell Marcos the truth
Someone whom the First Lady [Liza Araneta-Marcos] likes and whom she can get a long with
Most importantly, someone who is ready to be President
Someone who is friendly to members of the House of Representatives and the Senate since they will concur with the appointment

blocks.text: Franco also said calls for senator-judges to declare they would refuse offers may not exactly paint a picture of impartiality.

“I think there is no need for that call actually, since in the first place, no senator in his right mind will publicly say that he/she wants to be vice president even if they secretly want to be one,” Franco told Rappler.

“Moreover, having this call amplifies the talk that the Vice President will be convicted, but at the same time, if she is convicted, it is not because she is guilty but because some senators are aiming for her position,” Franco added.
No names have publicly emerged as possible appointees, but as Senator JV Ejercito puts it, discussing who will succeed the Vice President — at this time — may still be too “premature”.

“I don’t think it is proper to discuss who will succeed the vice president because her trial remains ongoing. It’s still too premature,” said Ejercito. Who will likely be the President’s choice, is the big question. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Philippines urges more equitable UN Security Council as global conflicts on the rise
articles.summary: The Philippines is calling for the expansion of the United Nations Security Council to between 21 and 27 members to ensure greater representation of developing countries and small nations.

blocks.text: October 27, 2026 | 10:36am
Philippines President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. addresses the 77th session of the United Nations General Assembly at UN headquarters in New York City on September 20, 2022.
AFP / Angela Weiss

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines is calling for the expansion of the United Nations Security Council to between 21 and 27 members to ensure greater representation of developing countries and small nations.

Enrique Manalo, the Philippines' Permanent Representative to the United Nations, pressed UN member-states to consider reforming the council to reflect the "contemporary composition of the United Nations and principle of sovereign equality," according to a Department of Foreign Affairs release on Monday, October 26.

The UN General Assembly held a debate on October 22 that focused on reforming the structural makeup and veto powers of the Security Council, the body whose mandate is to take action during major geopolitical crises.

During this discussion, the Philippines "reiterated its support for expanding the Council to between 21 and 27 members, while preserving meaningful opportunities for small and medium-sized States to participate in its work."
The Philippines also recognized Africa’s concerns on their lack of representation in the council.
The Security Council's five permanent members were chosen in 1945 based on the dominant Allied powers that won World War II.
These are the United States, the United Kingdom, the Soviet Union (now Russia), the Republic of China and France.

All five countries hold permanent veto powers, which gives them an oversized say in global security decisions. This has often resulted in deadlock when their interests clash with resolutions backed by the council's other members.
On top of the five, there are ten non-permanent members elected to the council for overlapping two-year terms.
Manila in June lost its bid for the single Asia-Pacific non-permanent seat to Kyrgyzstan.
Greater transparency, inclusiveness
The Philippines also urged "greater transparency, accountability and inclusiveness in the Council’s working methods," according to the department.
This includes "enhanced participation by elected members and stronger engagement with States affected by Council decisions."
Manalo also urged more regular interaction and consultation between the Security Council and the broader General Assembly.
Global conflict has reached unprecedented levels, with interstate conflicts hitting their highest count since World War II, according to a report by the Peace Research Institute Oslo.
In 2025, there were at least eight interstate conflicts – twice as many as the previous year and the highest number recorded since 1946.
Beyond the record-high number of interstate conflicts, the report also stated a whopping 245,000 people were killed in battle-related violence in 2025, making it the third deadliest year since 1989.
The United Nations' World Social Report 2026 had previously identified the veto powers of the UN Security Council as a major stumbling block to responding to major global conflicts.

articles.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon tells jury he wanted to report deaths but friend encouraged him to dispose of bodies
articles.summary:
NSW police officer accused of murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies tells court he wanted to do ‘right thing’ by their families

  • Follow our

blocks.text: Beau Lamarre-Condon has accused a friend of encouraging him to dispose of the bodies of two men “straight away” despite him wanting to report the deaths to police, according to his first statement to his double murder trial.
Lamarre-Condon, 31, is accused of fatally shooting couple Jesse Baird and Luke Davies with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024.

He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter. His legal team has argued that Baird and Davies were accidentally shot, and that he had acted in “self-defence”.

One of his friends, known to the court under the pseudonym Elizabeth Kennedy, had accompanied Lamarre-Condon while he allegedly disposed of the bodies, the trial has heard. She gave evidence last week that she thought she and the then-police officer were going out for lunch when he picked her up, two days after the alleged murders.
She denied in court helping Lamarre-Condon and said “I didn’t know anything”.
On Tuesday, Lamarre-Condon had a statement read to court that contradicted Kennedy’s version of events.

He alleged in the statement that Kennedy “flat-out lied to police in her statement regarding her involvement” and he wanted to do the “right thing” by the families of Baird and Davies because “they deserve to know the truth, too”.
In the statement read to the court by prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC, Lamarre-Condon alleged that after he picked up Kennedy, he showed her the bodies in the back of a van.
He alleged that he began to cry and then said to Kennedy: “I should just drive straight to the police now, shouldn’t I?”
Lamarre-Condon told the court that Kennedy replied: “No, no, you can’t. They won’t believe you.
“This is like Taylor Swift’s song, No Body, No Crime. We have to get rid of them straight away,” she allegedly said.
According to his statement, Lamarre-Condon warned Kennedy she could be charged as an accessory to murder, and he would not be mad if she walked away “right now”.
He alleged that she said she would help him because he “would help me if I ever needed … help with anything”.
He also told the court that while they drove, Kennedy played the song “No Body, No Crime” by Taylor Swift on her phone and “began laughing at the situation”.
He alleged Kennedy then assisted with carrying the bodies and helped pour concrete into the bags to help them sink after they arrived at a farm in Bungonia.
after newsletter promotion

“When the bag [wouldn’t] sink, [Kennedy] got my pocketknife out … and tried to cut multiple holes into the surfboard cover. This is where Luke got the knife wounds in his leg,” Lamarre-Condon said in his statement.
“Whilst [Kennedy] was assisting me on the farm, at no point did she say she didn’t want to assist or have any part in it. She was a willing participant.”

He said he initially didn’t tell police about Kennedy’s involvement in disposing of the bodies because she had begged him not to. He alleged he told her that if it went before court, he’d have to tell the truth because he “can’t lie under oath”.

Last week, Kennedy told the court she did not willingly help Lamarre-Condon, nor did she help to sink the bodies. While under questioning by Lamarre-Condon’s barrister, John Stratton SC, she said: “I didn’t know anything. I’m five foot and weigh 55 kilos so I don’t think I could carry a body even if I tried.”
Kennedy told the court that she waited at a gate while Lamarre-Condon drove out of sight to a dam on the farm.
She denied that Lamarre-Condon had told her Baird was dead. She also alleged it was him who played the Swift song in the car.
“He was the one that put that song on in the car … it’s a very niche song,” she told the court last week.
The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

articles.title: In Marawi, therapy helps mothers find new ways to connect with their children
articles.summary: Recovery efforts focused on psychosocial needs after the 2017 Marawi siege uncover the needs of children with developmental delays

blocks.text: October 27 is marked as World Occupational Therapy Day to raise awareness about how therapists help people of all ages gain or regain everyday life and working skills
When Sania Naga calls her son, Amal, for help, he answers, “Yes, Mama.”

It is an ordinary exchange, but one Naga could not always have with her firstborn. For many years, Amal was non-verbal. At three, Amal was not saying “Mama” or “Papa.” When he wanted milk, he handed Naga his bottle. When the television would turn off in a power outage, he pointed to it and cried.

Naga noticed that other children Amal’s age were already discovering words and sounds and becoming talkative. They could follow simple instructions from their parents. Others assured Naga that some children develop later than others, but she still worried.
Neither she nor her husband knew what to do.
“What will happen to my child when he gets older? What will happen to him when his father and I are no longer around?” Naga recalled thinking.

An opportunity to seek help came when Amal fell ill. During a visit to a pediatrician, Naga raised her concerns about his development. The doctor referred them to a specialist in Cagayan de Oro, roughly three hours from their home in Marawi City.
Distance, time, and then the pandemic became hurdles to getting treatment. When they tried to set an appointment, a year had passed before Amal was seen by a doctor.

Amal was initially diagnosed with cognitive development delay, a condition where there is a lag in thinking, learning, and reasoning skills. Naga asked whether medicine could help. The recommendation was therapy.
Getting it meant traveling to the nearest therapy center in Iligan, about 45 minutes away, every week. Amal had an hour of occupational therapy and another of speech therapy.
Naga arranged Saturday appointments around her job, her husband’s work, and caring for their two other children.
“During the first six months, I felt like giving up,” she said.

Then the therapist began noticing Amal’s progress. His behavior, once marked by hyperactivity, became more manageable. He became calmer as he learned to express himself more. At home, Amal began making eye contact and responding when she greeted him good morning.

Naga’s experience underscores the care and treatment gaps facing children with disabilities. The gaps span all touch points that starts from having their needs recognized, reaching someone who can assess them and link them to care, and sustaining treatment and support.

Data from the government’s January 2026 National Education Plan estimates that there are about 4.7 million to 5.1 million children with disabilities. Statistics from the previous year indicate that there are about 391,000 identified learners with disabilities in public schools during the 2024-2025 school year. Roughly 6 in 10 lacked a formal diagnosis.
In addition, a shortage of specialists and therapists complicates getting therapy and care even when assessed.
In Naga’s case, occupational therapy was one of the interventions recommended for Amal to help him develop skills for everyday activities such as eating, dressing and participating in school.
The World Health Organization listed fewer than 6,000 registered occupational therapists nationwide in 2025, with services concentrated in urban areas.
In Marawi, where Naga and her family live, accessibility is also a geographic problem.

In 2024, there were reportedly only two developmental pediatricians in Northern Mindanao. Families from Marawi seek care in Iligan and Cagayan de Oro. Appointment waits can reportedly reach three and a half years.

Jalil Usman, a social worker for Community and Family Services International (CSFI) in Marawi, said that intensified mental health outreach around 2019 as part of the recovery efforts after the Marawi siege brought them to parents needing support for their children with intellectual and developmental delays.

“There were gaps in understanding and, in some families, shame about showing others that a child had a disability. As families learned about available help and shared their experiences, others approached us,” said Usman.
“Some parents had assumed their children could never learn certain everyday skills, but it turned out they could,” Usman added.
CFSI secured funding to partner with the Medbay Therapy and Learning Center in Iligan to provide 21 children through 10 sessions each of occupational therapy.

Getting children to therapy became somewhat of a field trip. CFSI staff picked up some families from their homes and drove them to Iligan in an office vehicle. In the clinic, the parents would wait for their turn for their therapy session.
However, funding was not enough to cover the recommended 72 sessions. When the CFSI funded sessions ended in 2023, Naga paid for the treatment costs out of pocket.
“Sometimes, when we did not have enough money, we would miss sessions,” she said.

CFSI partnered with the Rehabilitation and Empowerment of Adults and Children with Handicap Foundation (REACH), a non-profit organization in Manila that provides free occupational and speech therapy to undersupported children and adults with disabilities. Together, they developed and conducted teletherapy sessions adapted to the children’s needs.
Through sessions conducted online or by phone or through other messaging platforms, therapists work with family members to develop home-based interventions using everyday or improvised materials.

“We often use toys, books, school materials, kitchen items, and other familiar household objects to make learning part of the child’s daily life,” said Archie David, founder and president of REACH Foundation.

A simple clothespin, for example, can help strengthen fine motor skills, while everyday activities such as preparing meals, sorting laundry, or playing games can become opportunities for learning and development.

blocks.caption: ONLINE. Teletherapy sessions adapt to every child’s needs. Photo courtesy of REACH Foundation

blocks.text: Amal’s occupational therapy program focused on visual perceptual skills, which are important for handwriting, copying from the board, organizing written work, and other classroom tasks.
Another child, Shoraim, had a hearing impairment that made spoken conversations difficult to follow in school. His mother, Sohairah Batabor, used gestures and written words to communicate with him.

Through occupational therapy and guidance at home, Shoraim developed everyday skills, including dressing, bathing, and preparing simple meals like his favorite noodles and fried egg. His daily morning routine is comprised of reading the Quran and praying.

“The most meaningful changes are not always reflected in assessments. Sometimes it is a parent noticing that their child is joining family activities more often, participating in class, communicating a need, or trying something independently for the first time. These moments may seem ordinary to others, but for families, they can be life-changing,” said David.
“As a child’s confidence grows, so do his opportunities to build relationships, independence, and a stronger sense of belonging at home, in school, and in the community,” David added.
Amal, who is now 12 years old, is attending a mainstream school as a Grade 3 student. He can eat, manage his hygiene on his own, and communicate with his parents.
Naga recalled the advice of the therapist to call Amal even when she needed nothing from him.
“Amal, come here. Mama wants to talk to you,” she would say.
Before, Amal could not answer. Now he does by saying, “Yes, Mama.” – Rappler.com
Disclosure: The writer and Abelardo David Jr. are both Senior Fellows of the Equity Initiative–CMB Foundation.

articles.title: Ex-FBI chief James Comey faces federal charges for third time
articles.summary: Comey's lawyers say the case stems from alleged disclosure of classified information to the New York Times in 2016.

blocks.text: Federal prosecutors have taken steps to charge ex-Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Director James Comey with leaking national defence information, according to a court filing.
It marks the third time the justice department has moved to bring criminal charges against Comey, a longtime critic of President Donald Trump.

Few details are provided about the two counts in the three-page filing, but Comey's lawyers said in separate court papers that the case stemmed from an alleged disclosure of classified information to the New York Times in October 2016, while he was head of the FBI.
Comey denied any wrongdoing in a video posted on Substack on Monday, calling the charges an "appalling abuse".
"It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the department of justice, one that we cannot become numb to," he said in the clip.
"Nothing's changed with me - I'm still innocent, I'm still not afraid of these people and I still believe the independent federal judiciary."

His lawyer, Patrick Fitzgerald, said in a statement that two different teams of prosecutors had investigated the alleged disclosure to the New York Times a decade ago during the first Trump administration.
"Both times the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone," he said.
The attorney said the court filing "purports to charge Mr Comey with crimes that he did not commit".
Comey was charged in Washington DC through a criminal information, which is a formal written charging document filed directly by a prosecutor.
This is different to a criminal indictment, which must be approved by a grand jury, a group of citizens sworn in to review if evidence is strong enough to prosecute.
Comey was fired by Trump during his first term, after the former FBI director opened an investigation into claims of Russian meddling in the US 2016 presidential election.
Since then, Trump has repeatedly called for his prosecution, and these charges are the administration's third attempt to do so.
Comey was first indicted by a federal grand jury in September 2025 on charges that he had lied to Congress during testimony and obstructed a congressional proceeding.
He pleaded not guilty the following month before the case was dismissed in November.
In April 2026, Comey surrendered to authorities to face charges alleging that an image he briefly shared on social media posed a threat to Trump's life.
The case stemmed from a 2025 Instagram post by Comey, which contained a photo of seashells on a beach arranged to read "86 47".
"Eighty-six" is a slang term for "get rid of", and prosecutors allege it encourages violence against Trump, the 47th president.
Comey denies any wrongdoing, saying he did not know what the numbers meant, and accusing the prosecution of political motivation. That case is ongoing.

articles.title: US seeks new charges against former FBI chief James Comey
articles.summary: The Trump administration accuses the former FBI director of leaking classified information a decade ago. Comey denies wrongdoing, while his lawyers argue the case is legally invalid and comes too…

image.caption: James Comey posted a video message on Instagram responding to the latest attempt to prosecute himImage: James Comey/Instagram/REUTERS

blocks.text: The US Justice Department has launched a third attempt to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey, accusing him of illegally disclosing national defense information in 2016.
Court documents unsealed on Monday reveal allegations that Comey directed a subordinate to share classified information with a journalist.
The case marks another escalation in President Donald Trump's long-running conflict with the former FBI chief, who has denied wrongdoing.
What are the latest allegations against James Comey?
The case centers on an October 2016 New York Times article about a secret US surveillance order involving internet company Yahoo.
The order reportedly required Yahoo to scan emails for messages potentially linked to a foreign terrorist organization. It had been issued by a secret intelligence court.
Prosecutors allege that Comey instructed a staff member to contact a New York Times journalist to correct inaccurate information published by news agency Reuters the previous day.

blocks.caption: US President Donald Trump has repeatedly accused former FBI director James Comey of wrongdoing, while Comey has denied the allegationsImage: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: According to the Justice Department, this resulted in the illegal transfer of classified national defense information to an unauthorized person.
However, the allegations have already been investigated twice.
Federal authorities began examining the disclosure in 2017. Prosecutor John Durham recommended against bringing criminal charges in December 2018, according to Comey's lawyers.
A second investigation, launched in 2019 under the code name "Tropical Vortex," was also closed without charges in February 2020.
How are Comey's lawyers fighting the new charges?
The Justice Department filed a legal document known as a "criminal information" in early October, shortly before the 10-year deadline for prosecuting the alleged offense.
Unlike an indictment, a criminal information does not require approval from a grand jury or judge.
Prosecutors say the filing allows them to extend the statute of limitations, which determines how long authorities have to bring criminal charges.

blocks.caption: A courtroom sketch shows former FBI director James Comey alongside his lawyer Patrick Fitzgerald during his arraignment in 2025 [FILE: October 8, 2025]Image: Dana Verkouteren/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Comey's lawyers dispute that interpretation. They argue that federal law explicitly requires an indictment within 10 years and that the government's filing does not meet that requirement.
They have asked a judge to dismiss the case. A ruling is still pending.
Comey's attorney, Patrick Fitzgerald, also pointed to the two earlier investigations.
"Both times the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone," he said.
Responding to the latest allegations in a video posted on Substack, Comey condemned the prosecution.
"It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice," he said.
"I'm still innocent. I'm still not afraid of these people, and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary."
What other criminal cases does James Comey face?
The latest case is the third criminal proceeding brought against Comey since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.
In September 2025, prosecutors charged him with making false statements to Congress and obstructing a congressional proceeding.
A federal judge dismissed the case after finding that the Trump-appointed prosecutor who brought the charges had been unlawfully appointed.

blocks.caption: Former FBI director James Comey testified before the Senate Intelligence Committee in June 2017 about his dismissal by Trump and the Russia investigation [FILE: June 8, 2017]Image: Andrew Harnik/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: In April 2026, Comey was indicted again, this time over an Instagram photograph showing seashells arranged to form the numbers "86 47."
The Justice Department interpreted the numbers as a threat against Trump, arguing that "86" referred to killing someone and "47" identified Trump as the 47th US president.
Comey denied threatening Trump's life and has sought to have that case dismissed.
Why has Trump targeted former FBI director Comey?
Comey was appointed FBI director in 2013 by Democratic President Barack Obama.
His relationship with Trump deteriorated shortly after the president took office in 2017.
Comey resisted Trump's request to pledge personal loyalty during a private dinner.
Trump fired him in May 2017 while the FBI was investigating Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election and possible connections to Trump's campaign.

blocks.caption: Donald Trump and James Comey initially appeared to have a cordial relationship before the president fired the FBI director in May 2017 [FILE: January 22, 2017]Image: Andrew Harrer/UPI Photo/Newscom/picture alliance

blocks.text: The investigation was subsequently taken over by special counsel Robert Mueller. It established that Russia had interfered in the election but found insufficient evidence to prove criminal coordination between Moscow and Trump's campaign.
The two men have remained bitter political opponents. Trump has repeatedly accused Comey of treason, while Comey compared the president to a mafia boss in his 2018 memoir.

articles.title: Bato’s wife defends fugitive senator: ‘He’s not an enemy’
articles.summary: The wife of fugitive Sen. Bato Dela Rosa issued a public appeal defending her husband, urging his former political allies and powerful figures to stop using him for personal agendas and to end what…

blocks.text: October 27, 2026 | 9:36am
Sen. Bato Dela Rosa and his wife, Nancy, at the Senate on July 22.
The Philippine STAR / Mong Pintolo

MANILA, Philippines — The wife of fugitive Sen. Bato Dela Rosa issued a public appeal defending her husband, urging his former political allies and powerful figures to stop using him for personal agendas and to end what she described as his "persecution."
In a Facebook post, Nancy Dela Rosa, Bato’s wife, said that he is not “their enemy nor the enemy of this state.”
“Thank you for helping me realize that there are millions who still believe and support him,” Nancy said.
“Please do not use him for your personal agenda. He has helped you in countless ways and he has done you no wrong personally. He needs your help, not your persecution,” she added.
On October 23, the government put a P50 million bounty on Dela Rosa, who has been in hiding since May this year due to an arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court (ICC).
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has also ordered Dela Rosa's arrest to be carried out nonviolently and lawfully.
Remulla said Dela Rosa was in Mindanao, being protected by a “powerful group” with which the government is currently negotiating for his turnover.
While Remulla maintained that the government can arrest the senator, launching a hard tactical operation is off the table due to the risk of casualties.

“We do not want a civil war to start because of our arrest of one man. We want to do it properly and we want to do it judiciously, and we want to do it cleanly,” Remulla said in an ANC interview on October 20.
The ICC unsealed an arrest warrant for Dela Rosa on May 11, ending his nearly six-month stint in hiding when he surfaced at the Senate.

Just days later, hours after a violent standoff on May 13 between Senate security and National Bureau of Investigation agents, Dela Rosa fled the premises early on May 14 aboard a van owned by Sen. Robin Padilla.

articles.title: Albay bridge stalled for over 15 years to open before Undas
articles.summary: The first two lanes of the Kilicao-Binitayan Bridge in Daraga, Albay will open on Friday, October 30, nearly five months after Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon ordered the completion of the project…

blocks.text: October 27, 2026 | 9:30am
The Kilicao-Binitayan Bridge in Daraga, Albay, which is set to open its first two lanes on Oct. 30, 2026, after being stalled for more than 15 years.
Department of Public Works and Highways via Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — The first two lanes of the Kilicao-Binitayan Bridge in Daraga, Albay will open on Friday, October 30, nearly five months after Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon ordered the completion of the project that had been stalled for more than 15 years.

Dizon inspected the bridge on Monday, October 26, with Albay Gov. Noel Rosal and Albay 2nd District Rep. Carlos Loria to check its readiness ahead of Undas, following President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s directive to make infrastructure projects that could ease travel accessible before the observance.

Dizon first inspected the bridge on May 3 and was surprised to learn that the project had been delayed for more than 15 years. He then ordered the acceleration of construction to ease the burden on residents who had relied on an old Bailey bridge to cross between Barangays Kilicao and Binitayan.

“Bago mag-Undas, bubuksan na natin itong first two (2) lanes ng tulay. Kaya naman palang mabilis eh, hindi na aabutin ng taon. Utos ng pangulo ‘yan, in 5 months, pwede naman palang gawin. Nagawa natin,” Dizon said in a video posted on the Department of Public Works and Highways’ (DPWH) Facebook page.

(Before Undas, we will open the first two lanes of the bridge. It turns out it can be done quickly, without taking years. That was the President’s order. It turns out it could be done in five months. We did it.)

The bridge opening came as the Marcos administration announced a Cabinet reshuffle on Monday, transferring Dizon back to the Department of Transportation (DOTr) and appointing Transportation Secretary Giovanni Lopez to lead the DPWH.

Presidential Communications Secretary Lino Cayetano said Dizon would focus on easing daily commutes, shortening queues at the Land Transportation Office, eliminating fixers and advancing mass transportation projects. Lopez, meanwhile, was tasked with institutionalizing reforms at the DPWH amid corruption allegations involving flood control projects.

The reshuffle reverses the changes made in August 2025, when Dizon moved from the DOTr to the DPWH following the resignation of then-Public Works Secretary Manuel Bonoan amid controversy over alleged anomalous flood control projects.

During his tenure as DPWH chief, Dizon led efforts to investigate alleged anomalies in flood control projects, including filing cases against contractors and department officials and blacklisting contractors implicated in irregularities. He also inspected questionable projects and testified in court over an allegedly substandard P289.5-million flood dike project in Oriental Mindoro. — with a report from Ian Laqui

articles.title: Trump administration asks Washington to set aside hundreds of ballots from suspected noncitizen voters
articles.summary:
This is the latest sign of the administration’s attempts to challenge states with competitive midterm races that could determine control of Congress

The Trump administration on Monday asked…

blocks.text: The Trump administration on Monday asked Washington state to set aside any ballots received from more than 400 people it alleges are registered to vote without US citizenship, less than two weeks after making a similar demand in California.
The announcement is the latest sign of the administration’s attempts to sow doubts about the election or its outcome in states with races that will help determine control of the US Senate and House.

In a letter to Washington secretary of state Steve Hobbs, the justice department said it had identified 1,500 votes cast by more than 400 people in prior elections. It asked the state to set aside any ballots they might cast in next month’s midterm elections until state officials can confirm they are legally eligible to vote. The state has more than 5 million registered voters, and the state issues mail ballots to all of them.
At a news conference, Charles Neil Floyd, the acting US attorney in Seattle, said he believed the 405 voters identified so far represented “the tip of the iceberg”.
“Because of limitations the state has placed on our investigation, we’ve only been able to uncover a fraction of the total number,” he said.
Hobbs said he was reviewing the justice department’s request. His office noted that the data shared by the department included the last time each of the 405 people voted. One was in 1994.
“The timing of this request – one week before the general election – is no doubt intended to cast unfounded suspicion on the results,” Hobbs said.

Much of the list was built based on “recent contacts” with suspected noncitizens, Floyd said, because federal officers are now routinely checking to see if the people they interact with are registered to vote.

Without access to those state records, proving someone illegally voted will be difficult, Floyd said. The justice department has demanded information including addresses, dates of birth, driver’s license numbers and partial social security numbers.

The effort is the latest by the administration to identify noncitizen voters, even though noncitizen voting is exceptionally rare. Donald Trump has repeatedly sought to undermine public confidence in elections.
Meanwhile, Washington officials have noted that changes in US Postal Service operations have disenfranchised thousands of legitimate voters.

The Washington request marks the third time this month that the justice department has brought a direct state challenge as voting is under way. All three states – Washington, California and Alaska – have House or Senate races that will help determine the balance of power in the country's Capitol.

The race for Washington’s third congressional district is one of the most competitive in the country in this year’s midterm elections. Democrats are counting on congresswoman Marie Gluesenkamp Perez winning reelection as crucial to their strategy of retaking the majority in the House. She has won twice in a district that also has supported the president each time he’s been on the ballot.

The justice department sued California as part of a similar attempt to require the state to set aside mail ballots from up to 20,000 people the federal government suspects may not be citizens. Another lawsuit filed in Alaska last week seeks to delay certification of the vote if the Republican incumbent doesn’t win.

In California, a panel of federal appellate judges heard rare Sunday arguments and questioned the timing, constitutionality and authority of the Department of Justice’s demand. On Monday, they declined to rule on the expedited timeline the justice department requested and sent it back to a lower court.
The elections clause of the US constitution gives state legislatures the power to set the time, place and manner of congressional elections.

Los Angeles county assistant registrar-recorder Monica Flores said in a court filing that her staff went through a sample of 200 records from the Trump administration’s list. They found the sample included canceled or inactive registrations, people with no voting history and voters who appeared to have been born in the United States.

California state officials touted the appeals court’s decision on Monday as a victory for voting rights. The state’s attorney general Rob Bonta vowed to “fight back against the administration’s unlawful overreach at every turn”. California governor Gavin Newsom meanwhile accused Trump of an assault on democracy.

The justice department told Washington it anticipates sending the state an additional list of people it suspects are not citizens prior to election day. It also noted that some of the people it suspects registered without citizenship may have since become naturalized.
Nick Robins-Early contributed reporting.

articles.title: After 14 years, P1.49-billion Ifugao irrigation project finally opens
articles.summary: The project was originally scheduled for completion in 2017, but limited annual funding releases, among other factors, pushed construction years beyond that target, a source tells Rappler

blocks.text: ALPIS. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. inspects the pump house and control rooms of the Alfonso Lista Pump Irrigation System (ALPIS), which draws water from the Magat Reservoir and irrigates 2,300 hectares of farmland across four barangays in Alfonso Lista, Ifugao, on October 26, 2026.
Presidential Communications Office
The project was originally scheduled for completion in 2017, but limited annual funding releases, among other factors, pushed construction years beyond that target, a source tells Rappler

items: The ₱1.49-billion Alfonso Lista Pump Irrigation System was inaugurated by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. after over 14 years of construction, aimed at providing a reliable water supply to 1,315 farmers in Ifugao.

The irrigation system will expand coverage from 275 hectares to 2,300 hectares, potentially increasing rice production from 900 metric tons to 26,000 metric tons and farmers' earnings from ₱16 million to ₱159 million.

The project is operational and will help farmers mitigate the impacts of prolonged dry spells, especially with the anticipated El Niño conditions, while local officials seek further government support for additional agricultural infrastructure.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

BAGUIO CITY, Philippines – A ₱1.49-billion irrigation project that took more than 14 years to complete was inaugurated by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in Alfonso Lista, Ifugao, on Monday, October 26, promising a more reliable water supply to 1,315 farmers who have long depended on rainfall for their crops.
The Alfonso Lista Pump Irrigation System (ALPIS), which draws water from the Magat Reservoir, is designed to irrigate 2,300 hectares of farmland across four barangays.
According to National Irrigation Administration (NIA) records, construction began on May 22, 2012, and was completed on October 7, 2026.

The project was originally scheduled for completion in 2017, but limited annual funding releases pushed construction years beyond that target, according to a NIA source familiar with its implementation.

The source said the project also encountered damage from several typhoons, right-of-way problems, delays involving the transportation of explosives needed for tunnel construction, and a lengthy process of securing approval for its electrical connection.

Construction-material prices increased during the extended implementation period. Pending clearance from the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP) also prompted an agreement to suspend construction activities in 2019.
The source, however, said the higher material costs and NCIP-related suspension had minimal or no effect on the overall delay.

Marcos said the completed facility would expand irrigation coverage from 275 hectares to 2,300 hectares and could increase palay production from 900 metric tons to 26,000 metric tons once fully utilized.
He also projected farmers’ earnings to increase from ₱16 million to ₱159 million, although the period covered by these estimates and whether they represent gross or net income were not specified.
“Alam po naman natin na ang pinakamahalaga sa pagsasaka ay ang patubig. Malaki ang pagbabago kapag ang non-irrigated areas ay magawan na ng paraan na mapatubigan,” Marcos said.
(We all know that the most important element in farming is irrigation. There will be big changes if we find a way to irrigate non-irrigated areas.)
The irrigation system will serve Sto. Domingo, Namnama, Namillangan, and Calupaan, farming communities in eastern Ifugao near the boundary with Isabela.

Its facilities include five pumping units, an electrical substation, a water intake facility, a transbasin tunnel, nearly 32 kilometers of main and lateral canals, and more than 14 kilometers of access and service roads.
NIA said the system is operational and will remain under the agency’s operation and maintenance.
Rodolfo Manglallan, president of the Sto. Domingo Irrigators’ Association, said farmers previously relied on rainfall, leaving their rice fields vulnerable to prolonged dry spells.
“Of course, magbabago yung ating sistema ng pagsasaka at nawawala yung pangamba namin na yung palayan namin ay matuyuan,” he told the Presidential News Desk.
(Of course, our farming system will change and our fear that our rice farms will dry up is disappearing.)
The inauguration comes as the government prepares for potentially severe El Niño conditions that could bring prolonged dry spells and threaten agricultural production.
NIA Administrator Eduardo Guillen said reliable irrigation would give farmers better opportunities to increase their harvests and improve their livelihoods.
He urged beneficiaries to conserve water and help maintain the new facilities, particularly as the government prepares for possible water shortages.

Guillen also noted that the inauguration came a day before the 44th anniversary of the inauguration of Magat Dam on October 27, 1982, during the administration of former President Ferdinand Marcos Sr.
More than four decades later, the reservoir continues to support agriculture, with the Alfonso Lista project extending its irrigation benefits to additional farming communities.
The severity and duration of the anticipated El Niño remain subject to continuing climate monitoring.
Ifugao Governor Jerry Dalipog welcomed the inauguration but also used the President’s visit to seek additional national government assistance.
He requested improvements to farm-to-market roads to help farmers transport their produce and improve access to schools, healthcare facilities, and markets.
Dalipog also sought support for completing the Ifugao Sports Complex and proposed a commemorative garden honoring Marcos Sr. in Lamut, Ifugao.
No funding commitments for these proposals were specified in the governor’s prepared remarks.
Marcos, meanwhile, unveiled the irrigation project’s marker, inspected its control rooms and pump house, and viewed agricultural produce displayed by farmer-beneficiaries.
NIA records show that as of September 30, Ifugao had developed 19,997 hectares, or 77.42% of its estimated irrigable land, leaving another 5,833 hectares for irrigation development.
The newly completed system is expected to help farmers cultivate previously rain-dependent fields more consistently and potentially increase their cropping cycles.

After more than 14 years of construction, its projected benefits will now depend on reliable water delivery, regular maintenance, and the harvests of the 1,315 farmers it was built to serve. – Rappler.com

articles.title: PNP: Still no surrender feelers from Bato de la Rosa
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police said it has not received any surrender feelers from Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, according to a report on GMA News" Unang Balita on Tuesday.

blocks.text: Published October 27, 2026 8:53am
The Philippine National Police (PNP) said it has not received any surrender feelers from Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, according to a report on GMA News’ Unang Balita on Tuesday.

“Wala pa pong feelers as of now. 'Yun pong one week na binigay for him to be able to surrender, ito po ay sign of goodwill for him to be able to end this with dignity,” PNP spokesperson Police Colonel Allen Rae Co said
(There are no feelers as of now. The one week that was given for him to be able to surrender, this is a sign of goodwill for him to be able to end this with dignity.)
This is three days before the deadline set by the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) for the senator to surrender.
Additional tracker teams have been deployed to locate Dela Rosa, according to PNP. But the PNP pointed out that authorities prefer for him to surrender voluntarily to avoid an unfavorable outcome.
Dela Rosa is wanted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) in connection with the crimes against humanity case involving former president Rodrigo Duterte’s war on drugs.
The senator is accused of being a co-perpetrator in the alleged crimes.
The DILG earlier claimed that Dela Rosa was hiding in Mindanao and was being protected by an armed and powerful group.
A P50-million reward is being offered for information that would lead to the senator’s arrest.
Meanwhile, the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) said it continues to receive information about Dela Rosa’s whereabouts and is pursuing leads to locate him.
“Para sa paghanap natin kay Bato, we will not leave any stone unturned. Lahat ng bato ay ating babaliktarin para mahanap natin si Senator Bato,” NBI chief Melvin Matibag said.
(In our search for Bato, we will not leave any stone unturned. We will unturn all the stones so we can find Senator Bato.) —Joviland Rita/KG, GMA News

articles.title: Opposition leader María Machado returns from exile to a Venezuela reshaped by Trump
articles.summary: Machado returns with Trump's blessing, even if Washington is happy with Venezuela's existing leader - at least for the time being.

blocks.text: Watch: Crowds welcome Venezuela's María Corina Machado after months in exile
ByWill Grant
BBC's Mexico, Central America and Cuba correspondent

Driving down roads lined with jubilant supporters from the western state of Lara to the capital Caracas, Maria Corina Machado's return to Venezuela could hardly have been more different to her exit 10 months earlier.

Colourful, loud, open and defiant, it stood in stark contrast to the way the Venezuelan opposition leader slipped out of the country in the dead of night in December last year to receive the Nobel Peace Prize in Oslo.

She had been unable to make it back to her homeland until now, thwarted on several occasions by the Venezuelan government - and by the Trump administration, which insisted the "time wasn't right" for her return.
Now, it appears, it is.

"Maria Corina is the indisputable leader of Venezuela," says 20-year-old Gregory Noriega, wearing a sweatshirt emblazoned with the logo of the opposition movement Vente Venezuela. "Her return represents hope."
Gregory Noriega

"This is a step forward in the electoral process which we've been waiting for since last year," echoes 18-year-old Hilary, who turned out on to the streets of the capital hoping to catch a glimpse of the opposition leader on her victory lap.
"She's returned after the double earthquakes when Venezuela needs her," adds her friend, Manuel. "The whole country is behind her to show that now Venezuela isn't scared."
Much has changed since Machado left Venezuelan soil to receive the Nobel Peace Prize.
Then-President Nicolás Maduro is no longer at the top of the Venezuelan government.
Maduro was forcibly removed from power by US troops on 3 January, and whisked to New York where he faces drugs, weapons and torture charges – to which he's pleaded not guilty.
He was replaced by his former vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, who has turned the page with Washington in ways few could have imagined.
The bilateral relationship is today unrecognisable from the years of mutual animosity during the reigns of President Hugo Chávez and then his handpicked successor, Maduro.
The new circumstances throw up some interesting conundrums for both sides.

When Machado left Venezuela, she had long been considered Washington's favoured alternative to Maduro. She returns to find the Trump administration perfectly happy with the one they've got – at least for the time being.

blocks.caption: Opposition leader Maria Corina Machado greets the crowd gathered around her vehicle on October 25, 2026 in Caracas, Venezuela

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
The Trump administration recently signed a major oil deal with Venezuela which gave the US a 100-year concession over a staggering 65bn barrels of Venezuelan crude oil.
The deal was reached in conjunction with a Venezuelan private company called North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP) run by a businessman with a chequered past, Alejandro Betancourt.

Machado has openly criticised the deal which the Rodríguez government reached with the US, albeit careful to direct her criticism at Caracas and at Betancourt rather than President Trump, to whom she gave her peace prize and whose trust and support she craves to move forward.

President Trump has repeatedly said how satisfied he is with Delcy Rodríguez, calling her "wonderful" and "a terrific person". This was the vice-president of an administration he previously described as made up of "narco-communists".
But the outpouring of jubilation for Machado's caravan into the capital shows she can still count on significant support on the streets, says Venezuelan political analyst Beningno Alarcon.

"The return of Maria Corina Machado, in my personal view, is the most significant [political] event since 3rd January," says Alarcon. "It means the most important political leader in Venezuela is back in the country."

"The reception for her return shows that her ability to mobilise her support remains intact, which means the opposition in Venezuela now has something very solid: a leadership which is present on the ground as opposed to solely in exile," he says.

Alarcon provides some evidence that the opposition – and the public at large – feel more emboldened since 3 January, a situation he believes will become only more pronounced with Machado's reappearance.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Political analyst Beningno Alarcon

blocks.text: Political analyst Beningno Alarcon

For instance, a joint study by the political think tanks Polis and Nexo suggests that Venezuela saw three times as many street protests in the first nine months of this year as in all of 2025, with demonstrations spanning a range of issues, from politics and working conditions to water supply.
Furthermore, there's evidence that the repression of such protests has reduced by more than half.
In such an environment, the return of a figurehead like Machado can galvanise an electorate that has spent years fearful of the consequences of speaking out.
Her return also needs to be seen within the context of the wider talks brokered by Washington between the Venezuelan government and the opposition towards a negotiated political solution.
Certainly, the US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, was quick to say her "safe return" to Venezuela was "the direct result of the US-supported reconciliation talks".

The Nobel Peace Prize winner still faces charges in Venezuela ranging from treason to conspiracy of insurrection. For years, she and her supporters have dismissed the charges as politically motivated and baseless.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Young supporters of Maria Machado

blocks.text: Young supporters of Maria Machado

Having made at least eight attempts to return to Venezuela by air and by sea before the Trump administration gave her the green light, Machado now knows she has Trump's blessing to be back on home soil – a position Delcy Rodríguez is both unwilling and unlikely to challenge.
She called Machado's return a "show" and the entire cross-country event, which was livestreamed by her supporters over the weekend, was studiously ignored by state television outlets.
But Rodríguez, too, needs a harmonious relationship with Washington if she is to avoid a fate similar to that of her predecessor and indicated she might be prepared to hold talks with Machado.
For as much as Trump has complimented Rodríguez, he has also made it clear that Washington expects nothing less than her full submission and malleability on key issues like energy.
Some reports have even suggested all major decision-making in the oil-rich nation is being largely dictated by Secretary Rubio via regular WhatsApp calls to the interim president.
The young supporters gathered in droves in Caracas to cheer Maria Corina Machado home say their fears of criticising their government or demanding change are vanishing.
Her return marked an irreversible political transition in Venezuela, they insist, one which they could barely fathom when she left for Oslo just a year ago.
Watch: December 2025 - BBC interview Nobel Peace Prize winner María Corina Machado
Additional reporting by Vanessa Silva in Caracas.

articles.title: Rodrigo Duterte camp opposes use of 2 witnesses' recorded testimonies at ICC trial
articles.summary: Former president Rodrigo Duterte"s defense team has opposed the prosecution"s request to admit the previously recorded testimonies of two witnesses at the International Criminal Court without…

blocks.text: Published October 27, 2026 8:17am

Former president Rodrigo Duterte’s defense team has opposed the prosecution’s request to admit the previously recorded testimonies of two witnesses at the International Criminal Court (ICC) without requiring them to testify in court.

In a document dated October 26, the defense asked the ICC Trial Chamber III to reject the prosecution’s application to admit the prior recorded testimonies of witnesses identified as P-1393 and P-1416.

“It submits, however, that P-1393 and P-1416 should be heard viva voce or, alternatively, pursuant to Rule 68(3), given the centrality of their evidence and the need for crossexamination,” the defense said.

“The admission of associated materials must likewise remain subject to the Chamber’s strict criteria and cannot extend to evidence that witnesses have neither meaningfully addressed nor explained in their prior recorded testimony,” it added.
In the alternative, the defense requested the Trial Chamber III to reject the request for admission of two associated materials identified as PHL-OTP-0003-1004 and PHL-OTP00247446-R01.
Earlier, the prosecution restructured its list of evidence in Duterte’s crimes against humanity case in connection with the alleged drug war killings.
The prosecution also asked the Trial Chamber III to admit the prior recorded testimonies of three witnesses identified as P-1370, P-1393, and P-1416, instead of requiring them to testify live.

Witness P-1393’s recorded statement attributed an alleged killing to payments allegedly made by Duterte to police officers. The statement also referred to alleged quotas for police officers and payments they supposedly received from funeral parlors for each body delivered.

“Also relevant is that P-1393 did not personally witness his [REDACTED]’s death or the events that preceded it. Rather, he has sought to reconstruct what happened and infer the reasons behind it on the basis of hearsay information provided by third parties who are not Prosecution witnesses,” the defense said.
The defense also cited alleged inconsistencies and contradictions in P-1393’s account.
Meanwhile, witness P-1416’s testimony was relevant to the prosecution’s allegation of a policy to “neutralise” alleged criminals.

P-1416’s recorded statement reportedly discussed his viewing of bodies and bullet wounds, circumstances surrounding the victims’ deaths, his attribution of the killings to police officers, and alleged payments.

“P-1416’s account also contains significant inconsistencies with the only other testimony regarding Incident [REDACTED], provided by [REDACTED]. Those discrepancies require further examination,” the defense said.
Despite its objections, the defense said it did not oppose the admission of the prior recorded testimony of witness P-1370.

“The Defence supports the use of Rule 68(2)(b) to expedite the trial, particularly in light of Mr. Duterte’s age and frailty. However, procedural efficiency must not come at the expense of his fundamental right to defend himself effectively,” the defense said.

Duterte is facing charges of crimes against humanity in connection with the alleged extrajudicial killings in the war on drugs during his term as president, and during his term as mayor of Davao City.
He was arrested in March 2025 at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport Terminal 3 and is currently detained at the ICC Detention Center in Scheveningen in The Hague, The Netherlands.
The trial for Duterte’s case is scheduled for November 30.
The ICC Trial Chamber III found Duterte, 81, fit to stand trial, stating that he “is able to effectively exercise his fair trial rights in the proceedings.”
The drug war saw at least 6,000 people dead, with rights groups believing that the number could be as high as 30,000. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: Australian politics live: Fatima Payman linking Haines-style attack to staffing allocation is ‘outrageous’, Labor says
articles.summary:
Follow the day’s news live

  • Get our breaking news email, free app…

blocks.text: Payman asks if PM is ‘waiting for what happened to Helen Haines’ to occur again

blocks.caption: Sarah Basford Canales

blocks.text: Sarah Basford Canales

At a late-night Senate estimates hearing, independent senator Fatima Payman accused the prime minister of being “petty” by not granting her additional staff members after she defected from Labor in 2024.

Payman has long argued her office is understaffed as part of a personal gripe Anthony Albanese has with her, but she drove the point home amid escalating threats of political violence. The senator told Guardian Australia last week her staff had also had to deal with human faeces being sent to her office, prompting the intervention of a biohazard team.
Payman said she had requested an additional adviser, in line with other independent political offices, two years ago but the prime minister had yet to process the request.

Payman said the extra adviser would assist her office dealing with the “psychosocial hazards” imposed on her staff since leaving Labor. A document tabled showed she had no advisers, which can be paid more, while most other independents have one or two advisers.
Payman continued, butting heads with the trade minister, Don Farrell:

double quotation markPlease raise this with the prime minister. Because if he cares so much about the welfare and wellbeing of people who work in this building, then I implore you and the prime minister to please look into the fact that my staff are burning out. They can’t take this any longer. Is the prime minister waiting for something like what happened to Dr Helen Haines to occur to my office, to me, for him to take our request seriously?
Farrell responded: “Look, I personally think that’s an outrageous suggestion, Senator Payman.”
Payman said: “I can’t believe that I’m saying that or making that suggestion, because it’s been two years.”
Farrell asked Payman to withdraw the comments but Payman said she wouldn’t until Albanese processed or responded to her staffing request.
