blocks.text: First AUKUS nuclear sub to come to Australia revealed
Washington has revealed the first nuclear submarine that will deploy to Australia under the AUKUS agreement, five years after the $386 billion defence pact was signed.

The USS Colorado, a 10-year-old Virginia-class submarine, will make its new home at Western Australia’s HMAS Stirling from late 2027, defence minister, Richard Marles, revealed in a joint statement with his US and British counterparts on Tuesday.

It’s the first of up to four American submarines, and one from the UK, set to rotate through the base while Australian Defence Force personnel get to grips with owning and operating nuclear submarines.
But Colorado’s arrival in Australia will be controversial because of outrage sparked in June over revelations the US would deliver lesser equipment than first promised.
Original AUKUS plans had Canberra receiving two used vessels and a brand new Virginia-class submarine before building one of its own in Adelaide.

The fact Washington would now be sending second-hand vessels was described as “trash” by Tasmanian independent senator and army veteran Jacqui Lambie, but ministers and top military brass at the time insisted used subs were the best option.
- Australian Associated Press

blocks.caption: Tory Shepherd

blocks.text: Tory Shepherd
UN experts ‘disappointed’ after major parties block bill to ban shackling during childbirth
UN experts are disappointed that bills to ban shackling during childbirth and strip-searching children were blocked by the major parties.
Independent senator Lidia Thorpe introduced the bills to the Senate, where Labor and the Coalition blocked their progress.
The United Nations Human Rights Council special procedures experts said in a statement that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women and children were disproportionately affected by the measures:

double quotation markIt is disappointing that parliament was not given the opportunity to formally decide on reforms aimed at protecting the dignity, bodily integrity and rights of women and children deprived of liberty. The failure of these bills to proceed should not mark the end of efforts to address these longstanding human rights concerns. We encourage Australian authorities and parliamentarians to continue pursuing reforms.

blocks.caption: Lidia Thorpe. Photograph: Jay Kogler/EPA

blocks.text: Shoebridge calls for ‘ethical Australian AI’ after cyber threat warning
The Greens leader, David Shoebridge, has said a report from the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) about AI threats to online infrastructure highlights the need for investment in another option.
He told reporters:

double quotation markWe need investment in an Australian ethical AI, which we can have some kind of comfort in, and not just simply relying upon these same US tech bros who are producing the threats to our very system … the idea that you invite the robbers in to protect the family silver is pretty bloody extraordinary.

The ASD report warned businesses and critical infrastructure must use cutting-edge AI models to defend against digital threats, raising alarms that artificial intelligence is enabling more dangerous threats than ever.

blocks.caption: David Shoebridge. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP
Penry Buckley

blocks.text: Penry Buckley
Minns says federal government must be ‘serious’ about meeting migration targets amid One Nation surge

The NSW premier, Chris Minns, says the federal government must be “serious” about meeting net migration targets as polling in the Hunter suggests Labor and One Nation are neck-and-neck in the key region.

A poll commissioned by Advent Energy, who are responsible for an offshore gas proposal off the Hunter coast, suggests support for Labor and One Nation at the upcoming state election is at 32% each in the region ahead of the March election. The Coalition was at 14%.
Minns was asked on 2GB this morning what he had done to lobby the federal government to bring down migration. Minns, a frequent critic of net migration under the Albanese government, said:

double quotation markThe best thing I can do is say what I’ve said privately, publicly, and I’ve said it on this program, and that is, we have to be serious about the target rate for migration and meet it. There’s no use saying, well, we’re going to have on average 200,000, a little bit more than that per year, and then it comes in at 300,000, because then people lose faith in the system. Now, in fairness to [the federal government], they’ve worked hard over the last 3 months to say these are the new limits.

The Albanese government has promised to achieve net overseas migration (Nom) of 245,000 in 2026-27 and 225,000 in 2027-28, while the Coalition says if elected it would more than halve Labor’s Nom target in the first two years from 2028-29.
One Nation has said it would have net-negative migration levels for three years, followed by a Nom “ceiling” of 130,000.

blocks.caption: NSW premier Chris Minns. Photograph: Steven Markham/AAP
Caitlin Cassidy

blocks.text: Caitlin Cassidy
‘Selective editing’ of estimates videos ‘humiliate public servants unfairly’, senators told
Female public servants are subject to “vile and misogynistic” comments underneath social media videos shared by parliamentarians, Senate estimates hears.

Jim Betts, secretary of the department of infrastructure, transport, regional development, communications, sport and the arts, was asked about a submission sent by the Australian Secretaries Board to a joint committee on parliamentary standards. It expressed concern that public officials were increasingly subject to “ridicule, hostility or abuse” when excerpts of proceedings from parliamentary inquiries were uploaded on social media “without context”.
Liberal senator Sarah Henderson pressed that “being able to highlight on social media and using the vision which is made available through the parliament is a fundamental function of this committee”.
Betts replied that there was already 14 hours of footage from Senate estimates yesterday that is now in the public domain, and the submission contained “stark” examples of selectively edited videos.

double quotation markThe concern that was expressed by the secretaries board was about the very selective editing of those videos, the overlay of commentary and other captions which were entirely designed to humiliate public servants unfairly … What we also find is … that the comment section on websites hosted by senators and other parliamentarians contain often vile and misogynistic comments about female public servants.

blocks.caption: Department of infrastructure secretary, Jim Betts. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP
Benita Kolovos

blocks.text: Benita Kolovos
Victorian Labor pledges to expand workplace protection orders to hospital workers
People who are violent or abusive to health workers could effectively be banned from hospitals in Victoria if Labor is re-elected.

The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, is holding a press conference to announce if Labor is re-elected next month, it will expand the workplace protection order scheme – that allows retail stores to ban aggressive customers – to hospital settings.

Under the plan, people who are violent or abusive to health workers can be hit with a workplace protection order (WPO), which effectively bans them from hospitals for up to 12 months. Anyone who breaches a WPO faces up to two years in prison or a $50,000 fine.
Labor will also create a $30m fund hospitals can apply for to improve lighting, CCTV and other safety measures.
Carroll says:

double quotation markOur nurses and midwives and health professionals go to work every day to make sure we have a healthy community … They are the heroes of our community, and I’m very pleased to say, under my leadership, we’ll do everything we can to protect them through workplace protection orders.
He says people subject to a WPO will “still be able to access healthcare” in an emergency but there will be “guardrails” in place when they receive that care.

blocks.caption: Ben Carroll. Photograph: Rob Prezioso/AAP

blocks.text: Aged care algorithm ‘fundamentally flawed’, Ruston says
Opposition aged care spokesperson, Anne Ruston, has urged the government to listen after a damning investigation by the commonwealth ombudsman.
She told ABC Radio National:
double quotation markWe’re really hopeful that now the government has this independent report, it will actually listen and say that their algorithm process is fundamentally flawed.

The ombudsman’s report followed reporting by Guardian Australia that older people were being left distressed and without adequate care after their home support needs were assessed by an “inhumane” algorithm as part of the government’s mandatory Integrated Assessment Tool.
Security reviews ramp up for MP offices over attack fears
Some politicians will receive security updates in their electorate offices after raising concerns about threats in the wake of the alleged attack on Helen Haines.
At least nine MPs will have security crackdowns accelerated for their electorate offices, the finance minister, Katy Gallagher, confirmed, after they raised concerns last week.
Security in Parliament House’s public places will also be stepped up.
Gallagher did not specify which MPs were affected.
– Australian Associated Press
Jacinda Ardern joins University of Sydney as lecturer and mentor

In news adjacent to federal politics, former New Zealand prime minister Jacinda Ardern has revealed she will lecture and mentor at the University of Sydney after moving to Australia earlier this year.
Based in the school of public health, she will host guest lectures and masterclasses and engage in mentoring.
Teal and regional independent backers were Farrer independent’s top donors
Continued from the previous post:

The top donor, Regional Voices Fund, backs independent candidates in regional seats while the second-highest donor, Keldoulis Investments, owned by Robert Keldoulis, is a major backer of Climate 200 – the funding vehicle that supports teal independents in getting elected.
Overall, Milthorpe spent $1,708,845 on her campaign, receiving $1,680,439 in donations and gifts.
Candidates endorsed by political parties, like Farley, are able to defer the campaign spending reports until February the following year when political party annual returns are published.
As a result, Farley’s electoral returns show he spent only $5,119 on his campaign and received no donations. This figure will likely be updated in February.
Farrer independent spent $1.7m on byelection campaign, electoral returns show

The independent candidate, Michelle Milthorpe, received almost $1.7m in donations from more than 5,000 donors in her campaign against One Nation in the seat of Farrer earlier this year, electoral returns show.

Milthorpe, backed by regional independents, including Helen Haines, ultimately lost the battle to One Nation’s David Farley in Sussan Ley’s former seat, 42.45% to Farley’s 57.55% on a two-party preferred basis.
The returns data, released by the Australian Electoral Commission yesterday, shows $670,653 of the total amount – or about 40% – donated was over the declaration threshold of $17,300.
The top donors for Milthorpe include:

items: Regional Voices Fund Pty Ltd: $215,000
Keldoulis Investments Pty Limited: $117,000
Keep Them Honest Pty Ltd: $75,000
Climate 200 Pty Limited: $61,653

blocks.caption: Independent candidate for Farrer Michelle Milthorpe. Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAP

blocks.text: More respectful discourse is ‘what Helen Haines would want’: Richard Marles
The defence minister, Richard Marles, hopes politicians continue to show respect and civility for more than a day, following the outpouring of support for independent Helen Haines:

double quotation markI really hope that all of us can do better … we need to really try and collectively engage in bringing the temperature down, and have a much more respectful and civil discourse. And I know that’s what Helen Haines would want.

articles.title: ‘Digital hostile environment’: AI secretly being embedded across Home Office, report claims
articles.summary:
Tasks from determining asylum seekers’ ages to border surveillance now involve AI, says Open Rights Group

AI has been embedded across the Home Office in near-total secrecy, reinforcing the…

blocks.text: AI has been embedded across the Home Office in near-total secrecy, reinforcing the so-called hostile environment for immigration, according to research.

Tasks from the detection of potential sham marriages to determining the age of asylum seekers and checking through the contents of phones of new arrivals now involve use of the technology, according to a report by Open Rights Group (ORG).

It is also being used to conduct surveillance of borders, through live facial recognition and AI-powered drones and satellites; to summarise asylum interviews and country policy information used as evidence in those interviews; and to prioritise and assess cases through the opaque Identify and Prioritise Immigration Cases (Ipic) tool.

Information for the report has been gathered from a mix of limited information published by the Home Office, freedom of information requests and questions from MPs. The report has cross-party support from Labour’s Bell Ribeiro-Addy, the Scottish National party’s Pete Wishart and the Green party’s Siân Berry.

The report, titled Automated Discrimination: Unpacking the Digital Hostile Environment, raises concerns about the use of AI in immigration, saying it is not neutral or accurate and can replicate bias and discrimination within society, particularly when a key driver for its use is anti-immigration policies and rhetoric.

It says AI is being trialled and tested in near-total secrecy, with officials routinely invoking national security to stonewall freedom of information requests and redact disclosures. Successive governments are criticised for pushing an ideology that reduces complex human cases to a technical problem that can be fixed.

The report raises concerns about “reducing people to data points” and replicating the hostile environment first envisaged by Theresa May as home secretary in 2012. “Relying on AI to decide who gets to stay here and who gets thrown back into danger is a deeply alarming move,” it states.
Open Rights Group is calling on the government to regulate AI and ban uses that are undemocratic and risk human rights violations, such as the use of ChatGPT tools in asylum applications.
It also wants more transparency and stronger freedom of information laws, a narrower definition of national security and a robust public register of government AI tools.

Ribeiro-Addy said: “In spite of questions and requests, the Home Office has been reluctant to publish the documents that would explain how AI is used in asylum processing, what the problems are and how they are being addressed. The department has not explained how it will ensure there is accountability when they fail or justified why some of the most vulnerable people, with the least power, should bear the greatest risks.”

Sara Alsherif, a programme manager at Open Rights Group, said: “Migration is a human phenomenon and experience, not a technical problem that can be fixed by artificial intelligence. We urgently need transparency, accountability and strict regulation to restrict how AI is used and to prevent its wider rollout.”
after newsletter promotion
A Home Office spokesperson said: “Use of artificial intelligence is just one of the tools at our disposal to protect our borders and does not replace or automate the role of human decision-makers.

“Asylum decisions are made by trained caseworkers, with AI tools used only to assist in navigating interview records and policy information. They cannot be used in isolation and do not make decisions on claims.
“We regularly monitor the performance of these tools alongside our established quality-assurance processes and have already committed to publishing updated evaluations on their rollout.”

articles.title: UK shop price inflation ‘highest since 2024’ as retailers struggle to limit price rises
articles.summary:
British Retail Consortium says ‘dam is starting to break on the huge wave of costs’ being kept from consumers

Shop price inflation has risen to the highest level in two and a half years,…

blocks.text: Shop price inflation has risen to the highest level in two and a half years, according to the British Retail Consortium, which warned that “the dam is starting to break” when it comes to retailers trying to limit price rises for customers.

The lobby group said shop price inflation was 2.1% year on year in October, a sharp rise compared with 1.4% in September, and an indication that retailers were beginning to pass on the rising costs of energy and food ingredients since the Middle East conflict broke out.

It said food inflation, which has remained low during the past year, increased this month to 2.9% year on year – against a 2.5% rise in September – putting further pressure on the chancellor, John Healey, before his first budget on Wednesday.
Non-food inflation, which includes items such as clothing and footwear, more than doubled in October, from 0.8% to 1.7% year on year.

The price of Brent crude oil reached $117 a barrel in recent days, well above the $70 average in the months before the US and Israel attacked Iran in February. Gas prices have also risen sharply, pushing the UK consumer prices index to 3.5% last month.

Until this month, retailers had largely absorbed the higher costs of raw materials, mainly in response to weak demand from customers. In surveys, consumer confidence has declined sharply since the summer, when it became clearer the conflict in the Middle East was unlikely to end swiftly.

Bank of England officials are expected to raise interest rates next week from 3.75% to 4%. If the rise in retail prices persists, it is likely to persuade many of the Bank’s nine-member monetary policy committee to raise rates still further in December or the new year.

blocks.caption: The chancellor, John Healey, faces intense pressure from Labour backbenchers to address the high cost of living in his first budget on Wednesday. Photograph: House of Commons

blocks.text: Helen Dickinson, the chief executive of the BRC, said: “The dam is starting to break on the huge wave of costs retailers have absorbed over the last two years.”
She said that while there was heavy discounting to attract shoppers ahead of Halloween celebrations, supermarkets could no longer keep the prices of tins and packets on their shelves from going up.
The chancellor is expected to come under intense pressure from his own backbenchers concerned that the high cost of living is harming many of their constituents.
The impact of cost of living pressures on low-income families is the subject of a report by Ruth Patrick, a professor in social and public policy at the University of Glasgow.

Based on a long-term study, it shows that high petrol and diesel prices are hitting families who need to transport disabled children to and from school and health appointments, and workers who use a car to travel to and from their jobs.
after newsletter promotion

Petrol prices above £1.75 a litre in many places and diesel often above £2 a litre can mean that work doesn’t pay, according to Patrick, who leads Changing Realities, an online project tracking 100 low-income families.

She said that in the last month almost three-quarters (73%) of participants in the project had shopped in the reduced-items aisle, while 62% had changed the food they buy and 63% had left the heating off even when cold.

One respondent, Rosie L, who lives in rural Scotland, said: “It’s getting to a point where I don’t know how we are going to keep managing to run our car.” She added: “Public transport is not accessible or reliable where we are [and] not having access to a car would affect every single aspect of our lives. Particularly as my children are disabled.”
The report involves in-depth interviews with 70 participants, of which 67 shared strategies they had taken to reduce costs over the previous month.

Patrick said the help provided by governments and local authorities so far did not match the scale of the problem. “The budget provides an opportunity to make good on Andy Burnham’s pledge that his will be a ‘cost of living government’,” she argued.

“Taking sustainable and long-term steps to secure the adequacy of social security would be a vital step here, and there is particular scope in restoring the real value of child benefit, traditionally a vital source of support with the additional costs that come with children.”

articles.title: Reader Q&A: After Lula’s sensational victory in Brazil’s presidential election, post your questions for the Guardian’s Latin America correspondent
articles.summary: Having lost the first round of Brazil’s presidential election to far right rival Flávio Bolsonaro, incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva spectacularly triumphed in the second. What comes next for…
articles.byline: Tom Phillips, Michael Hubbard and Guardian moderators

blocks.text: Key events

items: 24m agoWelcome to the Conversation

blocks.text: Welcome to the Conversation

blocks.caption: President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Photograph: Amanda Perobelli/Reuters

blocks.text: After losing the first round of Brazil’s presidential election to far right rival Flávio Bolsonaro, incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, better known simply as Lula, pulled off the most stunning political fightback in modern Brazilian history by winning the second, in so doing securing a fourth presidential term. It will see him become the country’s longest-serving leader.

The result – 51.79% to Lula, 48.21% to Bolsonaro – was delivered after a supreme court judge had extended polling time by two hours, and after Lula’s camp accused their opponents of sabotaging public transport in an attempt to keep their voters from the polls. It was the first time in Brazilian electoral history that a first-round verdict had been overturned.

But Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro who is serving a 27-year jail term for his part in an attempted coup after the last presidential election, refused to accept the result – just as his father had done, four years before. He called Lula’s victory “sacanagem”, a Portuguese word that roughly translates as “bullshit”.

Brazil remains a deeply divided country and Lula will have to navigate a hostile Congress, packed full of Bolsonaro allies, if he is to make significant legislative changes in his fourth term. His options are also constrained by a gloomy economic outlook, with Brazil experiencing soaring debt and entrenched structural problems. As he turns 81, will the re-elected president have the energy to face down the far right opposition for another four years and to lay out the ground for a credible successor?

And what does Lula’s latest victory mean for the wider region, and for the country’s relationship with Donald Trump’s administration? In the Guardian’s Opinion pages columnist Jordana Timerman wrote that “Lula’s victory shows that the rightward shift is neither inevitable nor irreversible. But the movement retains substantial electoral support, influence over the political agenda and a powerful ally in Washington.”

The Guardian’s Latin America correspondent Tom Phillips will be answering your questions on the election result, what it means for Brazil and the wider region, and what the country’s future may hold, here from 15:00 GMT on Tuesday 27 October. Comment with your question below, or email conversations@theguardian.com

articles.title: Lessons for the Philippines: AI content surge bypassed Brazil’s election rules — report
articles.summary: As the Philippines moves closer to the 2028 elections, Brazil’s 2026 presidential race gives a wake-up call: electoral rules alone cannot stop the surge of AI–generated political content.

items: Brazil's 2026 presidential election revealed significant use of AI-generated political content, with 60% of analyzed posts being deepfakes and many lacking transparency labels.
Despite regulations from Brazil's Superior Electoral Court banning deepfakes and requiring disclosure for AI content, enforcement remains weak, allowing for widespread misuse and disinformation.

The situation in Brazil serves as a cautionary tale for the Philippines as it prepares for its 2028 elections, highlighting the need for effective enforcement of electoral regulations to combat AI-driven disinformation.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Political maneuvering for the 2028 Philippine polls is expected to begin early next year, and Brazil’s 2026 presidential election offers a look ahead at the digital threat landscape.
During the first round of Brazil’s race, AI political content appeared in feeds nearly once per hour, according to fact-checking agency Agência Lupa.

Through its VigIA project, Lupa confirmed that 920 of 1,941 election-related posts were AI-generated from August 16 to September 28. Over half (60%) were deepfakes, which are synthetic media depicting real people doing something they never did.

blocks.caption: AI DISINFORMATION. Screenshots of AI-created posts during the first round of Brazil’s presidential election. Graphics from Agência Lupa

blocks.text: Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court (TSE) has regulated AI in elections since 2024, banning deepfakes while requiring disclosure labels for other AI campaign materials. However, the court ruled in September that the deepfake ban applies to content characterized as electoral propaganda.

The ruling came after the TSE voted not to penalize presidential candidate Senator Flávio Bolsonaro for showing AI-generated images of his imprisoned father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, endorsing him during a private Liberal Party (PL) convention. The court determined the photo was intended for a private event, not for public broadcast.
The senior Bolsonaro is facing a 27-year sentence after plotting a coup following his 2022 defeat to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
Lupa found that 60% of analyzed AI posts lacked transparency labels from post authors.

Even among the 40% of the posts showing disclosures, transparency was rarely voluntary. Nearly 60% of the labeled content were tagged by platforms, while native watermarks from AI tools like Google Gemini appeared in only 20 posts.

blocks.caption: NO AI LABELS. Screenshots of deepfakes posted on Facebook without AI disclosures. Graphics from Agência Lupa

blocks.text: Under TSE’s rules, candidates and parties must declare if campaign materials use AI. But Lupa discovered that almost half (47%) of synthetic media originated from voters operating outside candidate disclosure rules.
Official candidate accounts comprised only 24.5% of the analyzed AI content, while 27% came from anonymous profiles.
Agência Lupa founder Cristina Tardáguila emphasized that this lack of disclosure exposes how easily rules are bypassed.
“What we have seen so far is nobody cares about these rules. They are not being truly respected. And the norms, they are not being enforced,” Tardáguila told Rappler.

Lupa reported that 45% of analyzed AI content aimed to promote candidates in Brazil’s elections. Humorous or satirical posts comprised 27%, a category Tardáguila described as particularly dangerous for information integrity.

“As a fact-checker, you cannot fact-check humor,” Tardáguila shared. Humor is playing a big role here because what we’re seeing is that the politician’s supporters, if they want to play with a scenario that accuses the other candidate of doing something, they just appeal to humor.”

blocks.caption: [DECODED] When politicians meme their way into your feed

blocks.text: Direct attacks on candidates accounted for 24.6% of posts, while nearly 3% were neutral voter guides.

President Lula of the Workers’ Party (PT) was the politician most portrayed in synthetic media. He was depicted in humorous contexts in 39% of his cases, while 34% were personal attacks and criticisms of his administration. Only about 25% featuring Lula was promotional.

blocks.caption: SYNTHETIC IMAGES. Screenshots of AI-generated photos involving Brazil’s presidential candidates Lula and Bolsonaro, which have been removed on social media. Graphics from Agência Lupa

blocks.text: His opponent, Senator Bolsonaro, trailed in second. Unlike Lula, 40% of AI content featuring Bolsonaro aimed to boost his campaign. Humorous posts made up 28% of his cases, while 27% were smear campaigns.
Beyond political figures, Lupa identified journalists as deepfake targets, with synthetic videos showing news anchors reporting false survey polls or fake election outcomes.

blocks.caption: FAKE RESULTS. Screenshots of AI-generated videos showing journalists presenting false poll results. Graphics from Agência Lupa

blocks.text: Disinformation is not new to Brazil.
During the 2022 race, the Carter Center documented disinformation networks targeting the voting process and candidates, with Lula bearing the majority of the attacks.
Research by #ShePersisted and The Nerve in 2024 similarly highlighted gender-based attacks against female political figures during Jair Bolsonaro’s term.
What sets 2026 apart is how AI reinforced those tactics, triggering what Lupa’s initial VigIA report described as “an avalanche of content generated by artificial intelligence.”
Lupa recorded 64 election-related AI-generated posts published between October 1 and 5, a mandatory campaign blackout period set by TSE before the first round.

blocks.caption: MORE DEEPFAKES. Screenshots of deepfakes involving President Lula and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro circulated during the prohibited campaign period in Brazil’s elections. Graphics from Agência Lupa
AI biggest challenge of fact-checking elections around the world – experts

blocks.text: Tardáguila noted that while Lupa actively works with electoral courts to monitor synthetic content and alert platforms, a challenge remains.

“We have clear rules from the justice system, clear rules from the social media platforms. They are being fully and truly disrespected by all stakeholders,” she stated, adding that the “biggest loophole is the lack of [law] enforcement.”

Senator Flávio Bolsonaro led the first round with 47% of the votes last October 4. But President Lula won his reelection after securing more than 51% of the votes in Brazil’s runoff election on October 25.

blocks.caption: Lula, Brazil’s iconic working-class president, wins historic 4th term in dramatic comeback

blocks.text: Brazil’s struggle with AI political content offers a critical lesson for the Philippines, a country with a similar digital threat landscape.

blocks.caption: [DECODED] The Philippines and Brazil have a lot in common. Online toxicity is one.

blocks.text: Investigations into global propaganda networks, such as Cambridge Analytica’s operations in both countries, show how microtargeting and coordinated campaigns take hold not long before voters cast their ballots.
In response to these issues and the rise of generative AI, the Commission on Elections issued Resolution No. 11064 to regulate AI use in campaigns, requiring transparency disclosures.

But findings from the fact-checking initiative Tsek.ph revealed that deepfakes were still weaponized during the 2025 midterm elections to red-tag political figures and fabricate endorsements, alongside the spread of shallowfakes. Rappler also observed that deepfakes became a major disinformation tool in the Philippines last year.

Brazil’s experience gives a reality check for the Philippines: electoral regulations are only the first step. Without enforcement and accountability, the rampant spread of AI content will continue to bypass election guardrails, leaving voters to navigate an increasingly manipulated digital landscape. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Trump lashes out at Obama for joking that White House looks ‘like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory’ – live
articles.summary: Trump defends his renovations and jabs back at his predecessor before boarding plane for rally in Mississippi
articles.byline: Robert Mackey (now); Chris Hippensteel, Lucy Campbell and Tom Ambrose (earlier)

blocks.text: Trump lashes out at Obama for joking 'he's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory'

Before boarding Air Force One to fly to Mississippi for a campaign rally on Monday, Donald Trump was asked to respond to his predecessor, Barack Obama, joking over the weekend that his renovation of the White House, with “gold everywhere”, has “the White House looking like Saddam Hussein open a Cheesecake Factory.”

While rightwing media outlets have tried to cast Obama’s joke as a jibe at patrons of the restaurant chain – despite a report that his own family frequented the chain during his presidency – Cara Castronuova, a former reality TV fitness trainer now covering the White House for LindellTV, seemed to get confused about the talking point when she asked Trump for comment.
“Do you have a response to Obama,” she asked, “who made fun of the Cheesecake Factory, comparing it to the White House?”

“No,” Trump began before immediately reversing himself with a detailed, 500-word defense of his renovations, woven through with an attack on Obama, the nation’s first Black president, for supposedly being unbothered by “dirt and filth”, channeling a well-known racist trope.
“I’ve taken care of the White House. I fixed it with the finest artisans in the world. We’ve reskinned it. It was in horrible shape,” Trump said, in part.

“Guys like Obama, they would pass the front door, they’d see the broken masonry; they’d see the broken- the beautiful pilasters that were all broken, for years they were broken, and he wouldn’t notice because he doesn’t notice that,” Trump said. “He doesn’t notice dirt and filth that hadn’t been cleaned, where the walls hadn’t been cleaned for years. He doesn’t notice areas that haven’t been painted.”
“So it’s very easy for me to do,” Trump continued. “I do it very very simply because it’s my nature. You know, I’m a very clean person, and the White House was in terrible shape.”

“We have to explain that to Obama because he doesn’t understand it, because he’s not a smart guy,” Trump went on. “We have to explain to Obama that the White House is a symbol of America, and it has to be maintained properly.
“Guys like Obama don’t see it. You don’t see dirt. He doesn’t see filth. He doesn’t see broken ornaments on a building,” Trump added.

The president then turned to the camera to address Obama directly through the lens. “The White House - to president Obama – is a symbol of America. It has to be clean. The columns can’t be broken. The bricks can’t be falling off from under the plaster. And for you to say it’s a Cheesecake Factory, that just shows why you were a lousy president.”

blocks.text: Trump claims 'one of my top people got killed' in Washington DC before he deployed federal forces

Speaking to supporters in Mississippi on Monday, Donald Trump claimed that, before he deployed federal forces to Washington DC last year, crime was so rampant in the nation’s capital that “one of my top people got killed” in a carjacking.
“It was terrible, you couldn’t go to a restaurant. People would walk to the White House, they’d get mugged or killed,” Trump said.

“One of my top people got killed,” the president added, either revealing an incident for the first time, or fabricating a claim on the spot. “Driving up, I guess, waiting for his wife to come out of an office building, bring her home, and this guy comes up and wants the car and shoots him right through the head. Dead. It was terrible. And we don’t have that anymore.”

The president seemed to be referring to the 2024 murder of a former Trump administration official, Mike Gill, who served as an aide to the chairman of the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission during his first term.
'Nobody's ever campaigned like I have for midterms', Trump says in Mississippi

Donald Trump has taken the stage in Corinth, Mississippi at a rally in support of Republican senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, and began by suggesting that he is determined to reverse the historical pattern that midterm elections almost always go against the party of the president elected two years earlier.

blocks.caption: Donald Trump throws a Maga cap at a midterm election campaign rally for Cindy Hyde-Smith, incumbent US senator, at an arena in Corinth, Mississippi on 26 October. Photograph: Jonathan Ernst/Reuters

blocks.text: In a hoarse voice, Trump claimed that his rallies have “totally changed the dialogue” around the campaign.

“For some reason, presidents don’t do well in the midterm, no matter how good they are, even if they’re great, like us,” Trump said. “But I will say, nobody has ever campaigned- nobody’s ever campaigned like I have for midterms.”

The president’s remarks are ongoing, and so far have mostly moved on from attacks on the Democratic nominee for Senate, Scott Colom, who was campaigning outside the arena before the rally, speaking to Trump supporters on line for the event, to repeating his claim that the US is experiencing a “golden age” of prosperity. The president did not mention high inflation and gasoline prices, caused by his tariffs on imported goods and the war he started with Iran.

A three-judge panel of a US appeals court on Monday ruled 2-1 against the Trump administration, denying a request to block California from counting mail ballots from people on a list of more than 20,000 registered voters the federal government alleges are likely noncitizens.

The two judges who concurred on the majority decision were Mark Bennett, who was nominated to the bench by Donald Trump in 2018, and Gabriel Sanchez, who was nominated by Joe Biden in 2021. The dissenting judge, Patrick Bumatay, was also nominated by Trump.

blocks.caption: Sam Levine

blocks.text: Sam Levine

The justice department charged former FBI director James Comey on Monday with two counts of leaking information related to national defense, the third time the Trump administration has filed criminal charges against one of Donald Trump’s most despised foes.

The charges, filed in federal court in Washington DC, provide few details about what Comey is alleged to have leaked. The government alleges that the former FBI director leaked the information in 2016 and conspired with an unnamed person to give the information to a national news outlet.

Patrick Fitzgerald, Comey’s attorney, said the charges were related to a 5 October 2016 New York Times article that had already been investigated by prosecutors. The case was filed through a criminal maneuver known as an “information” – meaning it was not approved by a grand jury. While prosecutors will eventually have to have the charges approved by a grand jury, filing the charges through an information appears to have been an effort to quickly get the criminal charges in against Comey before the 10-year statute of limitations expires.

“Ten years after the article was published, the government filed an ‘information’ against Mr Comey that was not approved by a judge nor issued by a grand jury. It purports to charge Mr Comey with crimes he did not commit,” Fitzgerald said in a statement.

In a court filing unsealed on Monday, Comey’s lawyers argued the indictment should be dismissed because the statute of limitations had expired and it had been twice investigated and determined no charges should be filed. They also argued that the law required an indictment, not an information, within the 10-year statute of limitations.
NAACP denounces 'blatantly racist attacks' in Michigan Senate race

In a statement released on Monday, the president of the NAACP, Derrick Johnson, denounced a wave of Islamophobic attacks on Dr Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan, from Republicans, including Donald Trump.
Johnson said:

double quotation mark“The blatantly racist attacks surrounding the Michigan Senate race are unacceptable and disgusting. It’s the same ugly, divisive tactics we’ve seen used during the darkest chapters of the South’s history. Race should never be used as a tool to scare anybody or try to prevent them from voting their conscience. This behavior is grotesque and undemocratic, and cannot under any circumstance be tolerated from anyone holding or seeking elected office.”

blocks.caption: Shrai Popat

blocks.text: Shrai Popat
Reporting from Waterville, Maine

In Waterville, a town of around 16,000 people, Troy Jackson took the stage at a local theater, just a week before the midterm elections where he’s hoping to oust Susan Collins, the long-serving Republican incumbent, in the US Senate.
He was joined on stage by Elizabeth Warren, the Democratic senator from Massachusetts, who rallied the crowd of about 150.

“You know, we’ve had a medical emergency in Washington. Every Republican in the United States Senate has had their spine surgically removed,” Warren said, while blasting the Trump administration’s agenda, which has seen the price of gas and heating oil skyrocket across the country as the war with Iran continues.
Mainers are feeling the pinch acutely, particularly as the state braces for winter, where temperatures will soon drop to below freezing.

“Why is all this happening? Because people wanted more money. Billionaires had to have more money. I mean, it just doesn’t make any sense,” Jackson said. “It could end Tuesday … when we take the Senate.”

The US Senate race in Maine is neck-and-neck, with most polls showing Jackson and Collins virtually tied. In each recent election, however, Collins has defied political gravity, and defied the odds while branding herself as an independent comfortable breaking with the rest of her party (and Trump by extension). Jackson is banking on the deep-seated anti-Trump animus that’s sweeping the country to pull off an upset.
Trump makes baseless claim Lula's victory in Brazil 'looked like another rigged election'

Speaking to reporters as he left for a campaign rally in Mississippi on Monday, Donald Trump said that the comeback victory of Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, over his far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, “looked like another rigged election, frankly.”

“It was a terrible look, for the world,” Trump said, apparently referring to the court-ordered extension in voting hours after widespread reports that supporters of the president had been hindered in getting to the polls by public transportation outages.
“You know, elections have to be indisputable — and it looked very bad to me,” the US president added. “It looked so corrupt.”

None of the reporters in the limited press pool, after reporters from CNN and Politico were again blocked from taking part, pointed out to Trump that Brazil’s supreme court only extended voting hours across the nation by two hours after requests from both candidates.

The correspondent who was questioning Trump was Cara Castronuova a former reality TV fitness trainer now covering the White House for LindellTV, the streaming platform created by Mike Lindell, the election conspiracy theorist pillow salesman.

As our colleagues in Brazil reported earlier, the president of Brazil’s electoral court, justice Kassio Nunes Marques, who was appointed by the Bolsonaro’s father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, said that extending voting hours had caused “no change” to the election result.

Asked if he intended to intervene in any way, Trump said: “Well, I’m not running Brazil. I’m running the USA. And I just thought that the election was – I like Lula. I get along with him very well. I just think it had a very bad look, the election, the way it was tabulated. The extension given was very strange.”
Trump promises $1m reward for voter fraud tips the result in conviction
In a post to his personal social media platform on Monday afternoon, President Trump promised to pay $1m to anybody who submits a report of voter fraud resulting in an arrest and conviction.
“Anybody reporting Voter Fraud in the past Elections, or the upcoming 2026 Midterm Election, will be paid $1,000,000 upon the arrest and conviction of those that created the Fraud!” Trump wrote.

Trump has alleged for years, without evidence, that widespread voter fraud by noncitizens has tipped the scales in US elections, including in his 2020 re-election defeat. He’s made the issue a centerpiece of his domestic agenda in his second term, aggressively pushing legislation and executive orders that he says would root out illegal votes, but that critics (and the courts, in some cases) have argued would disenfranchise eligible voters and overstep federal authority.
While Trump is heading down south to stump for Republicans in Mississippi, JD Vance, his vice-president and one of his top surrogates on the midterm campaign trail, is heading west.

After a campaign stop in Montana earlier today, Vance will head to straight to Kansas, advocating for Republicans in both deep-red states as Republicans look to shore up their margins in races typically seen as safe.

In Belgrade, Montana, Vance was campaigning for Republican Senate candidate Kurt Alme, among others. He also laughed off comments Trump made in recent days commenting on the figures (butts, in particular) of both Jon Husted, the Republican Senate candidate in Ohio, and rapper Nikki Minaj.
“We’re self-confident men in the Trump-Vance administration,” Vance quipped. “The President’s been noticing a lot about the physiques of everyone lately.”
Israeli voters go to the polls in election overshadowed by war with Iran

Tomorrow, Israel will hold its first election since the surprise attack by Hamas on 7 October 2023 – an incursion that killed 1,200 people and kickstarted an ever-escalating regional conflict in the Middle East.

Since then, Israel has launched a series of wars against Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, while settlers have escalated state-backed efforts to displace Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. Under the leadership of Benjamin Netanyahu, the longtime prime minister, Israel has also found itself increasingly isolated on the world stage due to the scale of its civilian killings in Gaza and elsewhere, even as the Trump administration has stood by it.

Domestically, the coalition formed by Netanyahu has taken aim at democratic institutions, including the supreme court. Many Israelis have described this election as the most consequential in their country’s history.
It’s also consequential for Donald Trump, who launched the war with Iran alongside Netanyahu and has backed him for reelection.
My colleague Emma Graham-Harrison breaks down the Israeli election, and what’s at stake, here.
Lawsuit from news consumers targets Trump's restrictions on White House press

A new lawsuit filed in federal court on Monday against the Trump administration sought to end the president’s practice of banning or restricting White House access to news outlets whose coverage he finds unfavorable.

But instead of from one of the spurned media outlets, the suit originated with a different kind of plaintiffs: news consumers, who claim that Trump’s actions deprive them of their rights to “receive news coverage that is not limited by the president’s unlawful expulsions or distorted by the president’s unconstitutional threats”.

The five plaintiffs – who describe themselves in the complaint as a human rights advocate, a media watchdog, a historian, a civics teacher, a legal journalist and a student journalist – alleged that the harms to news consumers go beyond the loss of reporting from directly banned outlets. They said it also extends to other outlets that are pressured to soften their reporting, lest they face a similar ban.

blocks.caption: Donald Trump speaks to the press before departing from the South Lawn of the White House on 22 October. Photograph: Bonnie Cash/EPA

blocks.text: “Some of the news organizations targeted by the Policy have sued, arguing, correctly, that the First Amendment requires that their access be restored,” the plaintiffs wrote. The ultimate injury here, however, is to the democratic public.”

They continued: “Defendants’ Policy of restricting the access of disfavored news organizations deprives the public of the reporting of those organizations, and it inevitably deprives them of the independent reporting of other news organizations as well, since every journalist who reports from the White House must now account for the possibility that a critical or ill-advised word about the president may result in their access being summarily restricted or revoked.”

In his most recent and most sweeping attack on the White House press since the start of his second term, Trump banned three outlets – CNN, MS Now and Politico – from the White House, accusing them of peddling “fake news”. After a brief standoff with the wider White House press corp, a judge stepped in to restore the three outlets’ access while the case winds its way through the courts.
Judge rules Maurene Comey's firing from the Department of Justice was illegal

A federal judge found on Monday that the Trump administration has overstepped in firing Maurene Comey, the daughter of the former FBI director and Trump opponent James Comey, the Associated Press reported.

Comey, who was fired from her job as a federal prosecutor last year, alleged in a lawsuit against the justice department that the move was unconstitutional retaliation against her for her relationship to her father and her perceived political alignment.
Judge Jesse Furman, ruling on Monday, sided with the younger Comey, ordering that she be reinstated in her role and given back pay.
Read the full story here.
Former South Carolina Republican and Democratic governors unite behind Democrat's bid for US Senate
South Carolina’s former governors David Beasley and Jim Hodges, a Republican and Democrat respectively, have come together for a rare joint endorsement for Democrat Annie Andrews’s US Senate bid.

“This country is too divided, and the political rhetoric has gotten way, way out of hand,” says Beasley in their joint endorsement video. “That’s why we’re coming together to support Annie Andrews,” adds Hodges.
The two former governors, who once faced off against each other, acknowledged that while they don’t agree on everything, they agree on Andrews as the best candidate to put South Carolina first.
“Annie understands that leadership isn’t about making people angrier. Well, it’s about making things better,” says Beasley. “She’s willing to put people ahead of politics,” adds Hodges.
Beasley adds:
double quotation markWe may have served as your governor from different political parties. But we agree South Carolina deserves better than more of the same political fighting.
Andrews, a paediatrician, is looking to flip the seat, currently held by Darline Graham, sister of the late senator Lindsey Graham.
Trump heads to unexpected battleground Mississippi as Democrats try for shock Senate flip

Donald Trump is heading to Corinth, Mississippi today for a rally at 7pm ET, as he continues a closing midterm campaign blitz that has seen him dispatch to even some of the nation’s most reliably red states, which have turned into unexpected battlegrounds.

The Magnolia state, which hasn’t elected a Democratic senator since 1982, is probably not where the GOP envisioned needing a late-October stop from the president. But Republican senator Cindy Hyde-Smith is facing a stiff challenge from Scott Colom, one of many Democratic underdogs that have managed to expand the House and Senate battleground maps amid widespread voter discontent over inflation, the war against Iran and other aspects of Trump’s second presidency.

Hyde-Smith, who is vying for her second full term, remains the favorite in a state that Trump won three times by an average of nearly 20 percentage points. But Colom, a local prosecutor who would make history Mississippi’s first Black senator since the post-civil war Reconstruction era, is looking to parlay inflation, Trump’s lagging popularity and Hyde-Smith’s mistakes into an upset.

Colom has outpaced Hyde-Smith in fundraising since he launched his campaign last year, and he caught national attention this month with a viral ad that mocked Hyde-Smith, a former state agriculture commissioner, dismissing rising beef prices, driven higher by Trump’s tariffs and fuel spikes resulting from the war on Iran. The ad features Hyde-Smith saying that consumers “have so many other proteins to choose from” - followed by several characters declaring: “Pick another protein? I’d rather pick another senator.”

Colom’s campaign followed with a social media video that featured an AI-generated Hyde-Smith dodging questions about that controversy and other issues. The Democrat took down the video after the Mississippi attorney general said it could violate state law barring the use of deepfakes so close to election day.

Senate Democrats’ Super Pac, meanwhile, has been a late entry in the contest, with a $1.2m investment – a paltry sum compared to Senate contests in more populous states like Texas or Georgia but an amount that can go farther in Mississippi’s smaller television markets.
Trump calls Bill Maher a ‘total loser’ in 1,300-word Truth Social rant
Donald Trump launched a 1,300-word social media rant against late-night US TV host Bill Maher yesterday evening, calling him a “TOTAL LOSER” in a fresh assault on the media.

“Let’s talk about this COMPLETE AND TOTAL LOSER, Bill Maher,” the US president wrote. “He’s got a Low Rated Show on equally Low Rated HBO, which was once, long ago, a Network of Quality and Excitement – But that’s all gone.”
Trump’s lengthy and detailed post about Maher came after the host interviewed Karoline Leavitt, the former White House press secretary, on his program Real Time with Bill Maher.
Maher asked Leavitt about Trump’s “lame duck” presidency and whether the president would act on “vengeance” if Republicans largely lose to Democrats in next week’s midterms.

“I worry that if this election goes as badly as it looks like it’s going to go for him and the Republicans, we’re going to have a guy who doesn’t have as much power as he did … and we know he likes vengeance,” Maher told Leavitt.
Leavitt remained steadfast in her support for Trump and expressed confidence that Republicans could still outperform expectations.
Trump called Maher a “coward who is afraid to tell the truth about how well our Country is running”, claiming that Maher praised him behind the scenes but on television insults him with jokes.

“Also, turn your Laugh Machine off, it’s a joke when they laugh uncontrollably, even when you say nothing funny, and I’m going to have the Republicans not cover you anymore, because they try to talk about you as a guy who is transformative,” Trump wrote.

Trump has previously insulted late-night hosts and comedians on his platform and taken personal offense at those who make him the punchline. Earlier this year, Trump called for Jimmy Kimmel’s show to be terminated after the ABC late-night host joked about Melania Trump. Last year, the US president also called for Seth Meyers to be fired.
But Trump’s lengthy attack on Maher is notable, coming just about a week until the US midterm elections, where Republicans are trying to fend off challenges from Democratic opponents.
My colleague Ariana Baio has the story:
Catholic bishops say they regret joining Trump in Oval Office prayer
Joseph Gedeon

Two Catholic bishops who bowed their heads with Donald Trump in the Oval Office now say they regret it, accusing the White House of turning a private prayer into a campaign photo opportunity before next week’s US elections.

Archbishop Jeffrey Grob of Milwaukee and Bishop William Joensen of Des Moines, who were among the 12 bishops who met administration officials last Thursday, issued separate statements of regret over the weekend.

The fallout stems from the White House quickly posting video and photos of the prayer on social media, captioned as Catholic archbishops and bishops praying with the US president, less than two weeks before the midterm elections on 3 November.

blocks.caption: Catholic bishops, including Jeffrey Grob and William Joensen, pray with Donald Trump at the White House on 22 October. Photograph: @MargoMartin47 via X

blocks.text: Archbishop Grob issued a statement headlined A Public Apology, in which he said he felt “a heavy sadness” over the pain the images had caused, and that he had heard from people alarmed that he had unwittingly joined a political event on the eve of a national vote.

Others, he said, were hurt because of the effect of Trump’s policies on their families. “We should never have been put in that position by the White House,” wrote Grob, adding that he had harbored reservations and “wish I had heeded them”.
Bishop Joensen wrote that “many things tied to this present Administration” were “blatantly at odds with our Catholic faith”.

He said none of the bishops was unaware the meeting fell close to an election, but insisted that none had intended to endorse a party or candidate. “I wish I had been more shrewd and less simple, like those who exploited our meeting for partisan political purposes.”

Grob said the Heritage Foundation, the conservative thinktank behind the Project 2025 rightwing blueprint for the second Trump administration, arranged the meeting. The bishops, he said, were told it would be a private discussion of immigration enforcement, religious-worker visas and human dignity, with a possible chance to pray privately with the president.

After 90 minutes with domestic policy staff, they were ushered into the Oval Office, handed commemorative tokens and, Grob detailed, directed to stand behind Trump’s desk and pray. Nobody told them a video was being recorded, he said, and they never agreed to its release.
“I will be Senator Muhammad to you, bro”: Abdul El-Sayed to Trump at campaign event
Abdul El-Sayed responded on Monday after Donald Trump’s Islamophobia-laced rant against the Michigan Democratic Senate candidate during a campaign event in the state over the weekend.
During that speech, Trump referred to Abdul El-Sayed as “Muhammad”, playing up a Muslim stereotype, and accused him of being a jihadist with designs of instating sharia law in the US.
“I don’t even care that he remembers my whole name,” El-Sayed shot back on Monday, addressing a campaign crowd in Grand Rapids. “Because he can just go on and call me ‘senator’ after November.”
He added: “I will be Senator Muhammad to you, bro.”
Earlier, El-Sayed also accused the president of attacking him for his faith while engaging in self-dealing with allies in the Islamic world.

“I get that the president of the United States takes personal offense to my first name,” El-Sayed said. “He doesn’t mind as much when it’s a shared name from the Saudis who are funding his son-in-law’s private equity, doesn’t seem to mind as much when it’s the Qataris who are giving him a $400m private jet.”

articles.title: Agent of author Steven Galloway says sex assault allegations derailed promising career
articles.summary: The literary agent for Steven Galloway said it would have been "impossible" to sell any new work by his client in the years after a former student made unproven allegations of rape and sexual assault…

image.caption: Writer Steven Galloway is pictured in his former office at the University of British Columbia in March 2014. The former UBC creative writing professor's agent said unproven sexual assault allegations derailed Galloway's career during proceedings for a defamation trial. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia

The literary agent for Steven Galloway said it would have been "impossible" to sell any new work by his client in the years after a former student made unproven allegations of rape and sexual assault against the author a decade ago.
Galloway alleges defendants defamed him by publishing unproven allegations of sexual assault

Henry Dunow described what he viewed as the detrimental impact of the claims on Galloway's "promising" career during a B.C. Supreme Court hearing in the author's defamation lawsuit against his accuser and other defendants.
Dunow said he thought of Galloway as a literary "star" with a bright future ahead.
But the allegations, which emerged in 2015, derailed that trajectory, he said.
Galloway has filed the lawsuit against a woman known only as A.B. and multiple others. (Ben Nelms/CBC)
An author's "social capital" and platform carry great importance in the industry, in a way more than the words on the page, Dunow told Monday's hearing.
Galloway, the former chair of creative writing at the University of B.C., denies the allegations, and he was never charged.
He is suing his accuser, known as A.B., whose claims of rape and assault were found unsubstantiated by a former judge hired by the university.

items: 'Outrageous' rhetoric alleged in emails as Steven Galloway defamation trial continues
Author Steven Galloway finishes testifying at defamation trial

blocks.text: The lawsuit alleges A.B. and other defendants defamed Galloway by publishing the unproven allegations online and through other forums.
Several people originally named as defendants have settled with Galloway and offered public apologies.
Former UBC professor Steven Galloway’s defamation trial begins
The court learned earlier this month that A.B. was no longer asserting in her defence that Galloway assaulted her, rather that she reported he had done so.
The woman, whose name is under a publication ban, is not testifying in the case, citing mental health struggles.
Galloway, the author of The Cellist of Sarajevo and The Confabulist, was fired by the university and has said his career was destroyed by the allegations.
He testified earlier this month that he could no longer write, his income from book royalties had "cratered" and he was selling boats for a living.

Dunow told Monday's hearing that the allegations resulted in the cancellation of a $100,000 contract for a three-novel series Galloway pitched about a ventriloquist detective, meant to be a playful departure from his earlier, serious works.

He later agreed during cross-examination by A.B.'s lawyer Arden Beddoes that The Confabulist hadn't met expectations following the success of The Cellist of Sarajevo, though he said a so-called "sophomore slump" was not uncommon.

items: Steven Galloway testifies that faculty-student relationships in UBC arts program were common
Author tells B.C. defamation trial sexual assault claim derailed career, ability to write

blocks.text: The New York-based agent said he believed A.B.'s allegations had also thwarted the realization of a film option of The Cellist of Sarajevo dating back to around 2011.
The case has drawn intense attention in the Canadian literary scene.
A group of authors, including Margaret Atwood, signed an open letter in November 2016 calling for an investigation into how the university handled Galloway's case.
The court has previously heard that Galloway and A.B. had a two-year affair, which he has said ended in 2013.
Galloway testified she was a former student who was older than him, whom he'd met sometime in 2011 when she took a writing course from a colleague of his.

"I remain ashamed of having had an affair, period, let alone an affair with a student at the university I was at," he told an earlier hearing. "I should not have been cheating on my wife, and I should have not been doing it with a student."
A.B.'s former husband testified last week, called as a witness by Galloway's lawyers.

Atwood has recently penned opinion articles supporting Galloway, writing in the Globe and Mail that testimony from A.B.'s ex-husband saying he was exchanging text messages with A.B. about a hockey game at the time of her alleged 2011 rape in Galloway's office, was like the "Aha!" moment in a Sherlock Holmes novel.

articles.title: FTC and 20 states sue Dollar General, accusing bargain chain of overcharging customers
articles.summary:
Suit that cites 2025 Guardian investigation alleges ‘pattern of inaccurate pricing’ that ‘affects millions of purchases’

The Federal Trade Commission and 20 states have sued Dollar General,…

blocks.text: The Federal Trade Commission and 20 states have sued Dollar General, the nation’s largest dollar-store chain, for persistently overcharging customers at its more than 20,000 stores across the United States.
The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Nashville, cites a Guardian investigation published last December.
“Dollar General has for years engaged in deceptive conduct that harms the very consumers it claims to serve,” said the 95-page legal complaint.

“Although Dollar General promises convenience, low prices, and value, the company has routinely charged customers more at the register than the prices displayed on shelves, price tags, and advertisements. This pattern of inaccurate pricing has persisted for years and affects millions of purchases across the country.”
The lawsuit says the scope of the retail chain’s “pricing misconduct” is “staggering”.

The FTC is the federal agency charged with protecting consumers from deceptive, unfair and anticompetitive business practices. State authorities from Mississippi to Ohio to Nebraska to Utah have joined the case as plaintiffs.
Dollar General did not respond to questions for this story, but has previously said that it was “committed to providing customers with accurate prices on items purchased in our stores”.

The FTC’s allegations are consistent with the Guardian’s December 2025 investigation, which found that Dollar General stores failed more than 4,300 government price-accuracy inspections in 23 states over a three-year period. That article “was the subject of significant internal deliberation and discussions” within the company, the lawsuit said.

The agency noted in the lawsuit that Dollar General has policies in place that are supposed to align register prices with shelf prices. For example, it directs employees to remove and replace outdated labels on certain days of the week. Workers told the Guardian that, because of understaffing, they are often too busy to change those labels.
“Dollar General’s on-paper policies to update pricing achieve little in practice,” the lawsuit said, because “they do not track whether the printed labels are actually affixed to shelves.”
The FTC cited a Guardian interview with a lead sales associate in Louisiana who said: “I threw away tags sometimes, to keep me or a co-worker out of trouble.”

Dollar General told the Guardian in 2025 that it is “disappointed” any time it fails to deliver on its commitment to accurate shelf pricing. In court documents in Ohio, Dollar General’s lawyers have argued that “it is virtually impossible for a retailer to match shelf pricing and scanned pricing 100% of the time for all items. Perfection in this regard is neither plausible nor expected under the law.”

In a statement accompanying the FTC lawsuit, the federal agency noted that Dollar General markets itself as a low-cost alternative to other retailers, and that low- and fixed-income customers rely on the accuracy of its price labels.

“Dollar General has betrayed the trust of millions of American consumers and imposed significant financial harm on communities and consumers who are already struggling to make their paychecks last,” said Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC’s bureau of consumer protection.

In a separate case, the New York attorney general, Letitia James, announced earlier this month that Dollar General had agreed to a $1.875m deal to settle allegations that it had repeatedly overcharged customers across the state.

articles.title: Hamilton and Niagara awaiting results as polls now closed

image.caption: Rick McRae cast his vote at Prince Philip Public School in Niagara Falls on Monday. (Paul Forsyth/CBC)

blocks.text: A voting sign is seen outside Hamilton city hall.
(Justin Chandler/CBC)
The Latest

items: Polls are now closed across Hamilton and Niagara, and results are expected to start rolling in shortly.
Hamilton has 13 mayoral candidates, including incumbent Andrea Horwath, Keanin Loomis, who came in a close second in 2022, and councillor Rob Cooper.
There are three open races for councillor in Hamilton (wards 8, 10 and 13) and four open races for mayor in Niagara (Welland, Thorold, Lincoln and Niagara-on-the-Lake).
You can find live results for the Hamilton mayoral race here.

October 27'They've got to keep up with the infrastructure,' Niagara voter saysRick McRae cast his vote at Prince Philip Public School in Niagara Falls on Monday. (Paul Forsyth/CBC)Rick McRae of Niagara Falls said after casting his vote that he wants action on what he sees as a growing homelessness and addictions problem. Property tax levels are a "big concern" to him, and he is particularly concerned about what he sees as not enough investments into critical infrastructure and roads."They’ve got to keep up with the infrastructure," he said. "My street has had four or five water main breaks just in the last couple of years. They put off work for so many years. You just can’t keep filling in the potholes."

How the CBC News Decision Desk makes its projectionsAndrew DavidsonHello. I'm a senior producer with the CBC News Decision Desk, a team of journalists who monitor results reporting on Election Night with the goal of making projections. Why? So we can give the audience as clear a sense of who will run their cities and communities as soon as possible. We study historical trends and consume the entirety of news coverage on election campaigns, including tips from our reporters on the ground. When the results start coming in, we watch for advance ballots and day-of votes to report, and we monitor how much the lead for one candidate grows. When we see enough separation and are comfortable with the state of the race, we can make a projection. But we don't elect people; voters do. Municipal elections generally present more of a challenge than provincial and federal votes, since there's usually less polling information available on individual races. Sometimes, the races are too close to call, and we must wait for the results to go final.We take our time to get it right. A late night just means more candy and snacks for us. We count votes on election night, not calories.

Polls close in Hamilton and Niagara municipal electionsEva SalinasHi, I'm Eva Salinas, executive producer of CBC Hamilton, here at our newsroom. The polls have now closed. City staff told us recently that they hope the first results will start appearing around 9 p.m., although the timing will depend on how quickly polling stations finish voting and report their results. We will be bringing results as soon as we have them here. You can also find live results of the mayoral race in Hamilton here.

October 26What voter turnout looked like in 2022Jeffery TramVoter turnout in the 2022 municipal election was 35.38 per cent, with 143,375 ballots cast out of 405,288 eligible voters. Although the turnout percentage fell compared to 2018, the number of voters was higher than the previous election and the highest total since 2000, according to the City of Hamilton.Peter Graefe, a professor in McMaster University's department of political science, told CBC Hamilton he is concerned fewer people may be following this election than last time. "It's hard to know whether Hamiltonians really know there's an election going on beyond the signs," he said.Karen Bird, another McMaster politics expert, said she worries about voter engagement this election, particularly among young people.

More than 30,000 people voted in Hamilton before todayJeffery TramA voting sign outside St. Thomas More Catholic Secondary School in Hamilton's Ward 14. (Saira Peesker/CBC)We're expecting most voting to take place today, but thousands of people have already cast their ballots.The City of Hamilton says 34,996 people voted during the first three weeks of advance voting, including 15,632 over the weekend of Oct. 17 and 18. That exceeds the 30,893 ballots cast over four days of advance voting in 2022. The numbers are reflective of the city's efforts to expand its options for voting ahead of election day. This includes a ballot-on-demand service that allows eligible voters to cast a ballot from a location regardless of which ward they live in. Ballots cast at advance polls and ballot-on-demand locations will be counted today.

Polling day 'snuck up on us,' voter says of a low-profile election seasonJustin ChandlerJonathan Deveau cast his ballot at Dr. J. E. Davey Elementary School on Monday election night in Hamilton. (Carlos Osorio/CBC)Jonathan Deveau, 42, voted in downtown Hamilton around 7:30 p.m. He said crime and homelessness were top of mind for him this election. He said didn’t hear many people talking about the election. "It felt like it snuck up on us."

Some candidates are already acclaimedJustin ChandlerSome candidates win before anyone even votes. That's called acclamation, and it's the process that happens when a candidate is the only one running for an elected office and wins by default. In Hamilton, more than a third of school board trustees were acclaimed, with one saying a shortage of candidates "isn't healthy for democracy."On the Hamilton-Wentworth District School Board, candidates for two of 11 seats won by acclamation:Incumbent Abby Zaitley in Ward 4.In Ward 13 Chris Slye was acclaimed when Andrea Wappel's name was withdrawn.At the Hamilton-Wentworth Catholic District School Board, candidates for four of the nine seats won by acclamation:Mark Valvasori, who was acclaimed in 2022, was again acclaimed for wards 1, 2 and 15.Ralph Agostino was acclaimed in wards 3 and 4.Incumbent Aldo D'Intino was acclaimed in Ward 5.In wards 9 and 11, current Ward 7 trustee Tyler Iorio was acclaimed.Nathalie Dufour Seguin was acclaimed for the French Catholic board trustee seat.The French public board trustee seat went to Sonia Macaluso, after the only other candidate, Pierre Gregory, withdrew.The eight acclamations on the school boards was four times higher than in 2022.The Association of Municipalities of Ontario said there were 400 candidate acclamations across the province in 2026, down from 548 in 2022 and 477 in 2018.

How will votes be counted?Jeffery TramWhen polls close at 8 p.m. in Hamilton, anyone still in line will be eligible to vote. Election workers will identify the end of the line and allow everyone present to finish voting before closing up.Throughout the day, workers feed marked ballots into a tabulator, which record votes. Paper ballots will be dropped into secure boxes.At the end of the day, the tabulators will print results showing the votes recorded by each machine.It is then sent to a central location, where the city will then start posting the results.Some polling locations experienced delays during the 2022 municipal election because of problems with software used to manage the voters' list. The system's servers slowed down, making it harder for staff to process voters quickly, the city has told us. This year, the city has an offline version of the software it can switch to if needed, along with backup internet connections and IT staff assigned to every ward.

Exciting races to watch across the regionJustin ChandlerBurlington city hall is seen in 2025. (Kate Bueckert/CBC)Had your fill of Hamilton's hot mayoral race? Things are nearly just as spicy in neighbouring Burlington, where two incumbent councillors — Lisa Kearns and Rory Nisan — are challenging the incumbent mayor, Marianne Meed Ward. With three of six sitting councillors not running for re-election, that city is sure to see new faces in the council chamber. There are at least three new Hamilton city councillors heading to city hall, as wards 8, 10 and 13 are without incumbents. In Ward 8, residents will get their third councillor in just over a year, as Rob Cooper is running for mayor instead of the council seat. In Ward 10, 11 candidates vying to replace Jeff Beattie, who ran and won a recent provincial byelection, becoming an MPP. And, in Ward 13, four candidates are facing off to replace Alex Wilson, who opted not to run again. Brantford is guaranteed to get a new mayor, with incumbent Kevin Davis not running again. There are seven candidates in that race, including three city councillors, a business owner and a wrestler. The mayor of Norfolk County, Amy Martin, also chose not to run again. There, seven candidates are running for mayor. And, in Haldimand County, three challengers are trying to beat the incumbent mayor, Shelley Ann Bentley.

This election sees a big change in NiagaraPaul ForsythA collage of election sign clusters along roadways in Niagara Falls. (Paul Forsyth/CBC)I'm Paul Forsyth, a CBC News reporter based in Niagara. I'll be watching what's shaping up to be some interesting election races in this region.One of the biggest changes is there are no choices for regional council for the first time in 56 years, because the Ontario government is eliminating the 19 region-only council positions. That means only the 12 Niagara mayors will sit on regional council, along with a provincially-appointed chair.Thorold, Niagara-on-the-Lake and Lincoln are all guaranteed to get new mayors because their incumbent mayors didn't run for re-election.The same is true in Welland, which has the hottest mayoral race. Eight people are vying to claim the seat left vacant by outgoing Mayor Frank Campion. In smaller Wainfleet, there's even a grudge match: former mayor Kevin Gibson, who was narrowly defeated in 2022 by current Mayor Brian Grant, is the sole challenger to Grant in this election.
