articles.title: Why Ukraine may be involved in Mali's conflict
articles.summary: Allegations that Ukrainian specialists are supporting Tuareg rebels in Mali highlight Kyiv's effort to challenge Russian influence far beyond the battlefield in Europe.

image.caption: There are growing indications that Ukraine is providing military support to Tuareg rebels and jihadists in MaliImage: Souleymane Ag Anara/AFP

blocks.text: Ukraine is fighting Russia — and the conflict may extend into Africa's Sahel region.

According to an investigation published by US media outlet CNN in September, around 15 Ukrainian drone specialists are reportedly supporting Tuareg rebels in northern Mali. Their common enemy: the military government in Bamako and its Russian allies.
But how reliable is the information? And what price could Kyiv pay for engaging in Africa?

Marta Oliynyk-D'omochko, coordinator of the African Studies Program at the National University of Kyiv-Mohyla Academy, sees a strategic motive. "Ukraine's main interest is to weaken Russia's influence around the world," she told DW. If Russia's military influence were rolled back, she added, the economic opportunities arising from it would also diminish.

Russian historian Irina Filatova, professor emeritus at the University of KwaZulu-Natal in South Africa, also considers Ukrainian support for the Tuareg movement plausible. However, she said she has no independent evidence to confirm such involvement.

Kyiv's alleged partners are controversial. The Tuareg separatist Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) cooperates with the Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal Muslimeen (JNIM), a jihadist group affiliated with al-Qaeda.
Suspicions dating back to 2024
In July 2024, DW reported on possible involvement by the Ukrainian military intelligence service (HUR) in an ambush on Russian Wagner fighters near Tinzaouaten in northern Mali.
At the time, HUR spokesperson Andriy Yusov said the Tuareg rebels had received information they needed to carry out the attack. Ukraine denied direct involvement.
Jihadist groups in Africa and their links
Paramilitaries from Russia's Wagner Group and Malian troops suffered heavy losses in the July 2024 attack.
CNN's investigation has reignited the question of whether the Russia-Ukraine war is also being fought on African soil.
Signals from Kyiv, but no confirmation

The suspicions were renewed by a post on X by Kyrylo Budanov. The former head of Ukraine's military intelligence, now chief of staff to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote on September 7 that Ukrainian intelligence protects the country's interests worldwide — "from Russia to Africa … in the burning desert sands and in the snows of icy Antarctica...".

Budanov did not explicitly mention Mali and his post does not confirm any specific operation. CNN reported that the Ukrainians provided drone training, operational planning and remote support for drone missions. DW has not independently verified those claims.

DW reached out to the HUR for comment. Among other things, DW wanted to know whether personnel had been deployed to Mali, whether the political leadership had approved such a mission, and what measures were in place to ensure that the JNIM — which cooperates with the FLA — does not indirectly benefit from Ukrainian support.
DW did not receive a specific response. An HUR spokesperson said the agency might provide information at a later date. The extent of any potential Ukrainian involvement therefore remains unclear.
Why Mali matters to Kyiv

Following military coups in 2020 and 2021, Mali increasingly turned away from Western partners and toward Russia. The Wagner Group was subsequently replaced by the Africa Corps in 2025 as Moscow reorganized its military presence.
Russia has sought to consolidate its influence in the Sahel region and present itself as a reliable security partner.
Ulf Laessing, former head of the Sahel program of the Konrad Adenauer Foundation in Mali and now head of its Syria and Iraq program, said Russia is continuing to expand its activities in Africa.

"I have received information that the Africa Corps still uses Syria and Libya as transit points for flights from Russia, including for refueling and loading, to support its operations on the continent," Laessing told DW.
How could Wagner Group revolt impact Africa?
From Ukraine's perspective, it could be attractive to exert pressure on Russian forces in Africa.

Filatova sees a strategic logic to this: "The Ukrainians regard Russian troops anywhere in the world as legitimate targets." Setbacks in Mali could tie up Russian resources and undermine Moscow's reputation as a security partner, she argued.

However, Oliynyk-D'omochko stressed that the relationship with the Tuareg is not a comprehensive alliance. The FLA is not seeking to replace the government in Bamako. Instead, it is focused on northern Mali and is pursuing self-determination or extensive autonomy.
Oliynyk-D'omochko describes the relationship as a tactical arrangement: "It is more of a situational alliance against a common enemy than a comprehensive partnership."
The alliance with jihadists

The FLA is fighting for an independent state in the north of Mali, a region predominantly inhabited by Tuaregs. JNIM, by contrast, aims to impose strict Islamic rule. Both groups oppose the military government and its Russian allies, but their objectives differ.

Any potential Ukrainian support for the FLA would not, in itself, prove that Kyiv is directly supporting JNIM. However, jihadists could benefit indirectly if they conduct joint operations with FLA or gain access to knowledge and equipment.
Cooperation between Tuareg and Islamist groups dates back more than a decade.

After the ousting and killing of Libya's longtime dictator Muammar al-Gaddafi during the Arab Spring in October 2011, heavily armed Tuareg fighters returned to Mali and took up the struggle for an independent state.
In the process, separatist ambitions became intertwined with Islamist movements. Iyad Ag Ghaly, the current leader of JNIM, was himself involved in the Tuareg rebellion before turning to jihadism.

According to Oliynyk-D'omochko, the cooperation is primarily tactical in nature. The two sides have collaborated during past uprisings but later fell out. It remains unclear how long the current alliance will last.

For Kyiv, this also poses a political risk. In many African countries, the Tuaregs are viewed as separatists. Cooperation with them could therefore create the impression that Ukraine is interfering in another country's internal affairs.
Claims of support for armed groups

Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso accuse Ukraine of supporting armed groups and threatening their territorial integrity. The three Sahel nations, all ruled by military governments, have severed diplomatic relations with Kyiv and deepened their cooperation with Russia.

In September, Mali's Foreign Minister Abdoulaye Diop accused Ukraine at the United Nations of "providing clear and open support to terrorist groups and other mafia-like groups to undermine our country's territorial integrity," reported Agence France-Presse. Diop did not provide evidence for his claim.
The three nations' governments have may have an interest in legitimizing their partnership with Moscow and portraying Kyiv as a destabilizing actor.

Oliynyk-D'omochko has found no definitive proof of the allegations, yet warned of the potential consequences for Ukraine's Africa policy. Kyiv advocates equal partnerships with African countries. Any alleged cooperation with separatists could undermine that message and affect how potential partners view Ukraine.
What price could Ukraine pay?

Engagement in Mali could offer Ukraine a relatively low-cost way to weaken Russian interests beyond Europe. A small team of specialists could train local fighters and improve their capabilities in the use of drones.

But a potential partnership with the FLA carries political risks. Because the Tuareg separatists cooperate with the JNIM, Kyiv could face accusations of indirectly supporting jihadist fighters. That could undermine Ukraine's efforts to strengthen its relations with African countries.
How Mali's big bet on Russia is backfiring

articles.title: Audi boss under fire in Germany for Trump rally appearance
articles.summary:
Gernot Döllner criticised for in-person announcement of major investment in US days before midterm elections

The head of the luxury carmaker Audi is under fire in Germany for appearing at a…

blocks.text: The head of the luxury carmaker Audi is under fire in Germany for appearing at a rally with Donald Trump just days before the US midterm elections, to announce billions of dollars of investment in battleground state Georgia.

Gernot Döllner joined Trump on stage after the US president gave a speech criticised by the head of an elected body of employees at Audi’s parent company, Volkswagen, as being full of “racism, sexism, transphobia [and] contempt for democracy”.

Daniela Cavallo, the head of the VW works council, added that anyone who heard Trump’s speech and then saw that Döllner had become an active participant in the event must “sink into the ground with shame”, according to internal company communications released to German media.
She said the investment deal and Döllner’s appearance showed VW’s management had allowed itself to be “turned into a puppet in the propaganda show of a highly dubious political figure”.

Isabel Cademartori, the transport spokesperson for Germany’s Social Democrats – part of the country’s ruling coalition – called Döllner’s actions a “disgrace”. She added this was particularly so “in view of the history of the Volkswagen Group”, in an apparent reference to VW’s founding as a showcase company under the Nazis.

A spokesperson for the German government declined to comment on the matter, calling it “a business decision regarding where the company invests and, in this case, where the company’s chief executive appears”.

blocks.caption: Döllner announced plans to spend $4bn and create 4,500 jobs in the battleground state of Georgia. Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/AP

blocks.text: Döllner and Trump announced to the crowd on Saturday that Audi would spend $4bn to build its first factory in the US and create 4,500 jobs, even as VW aims to slash tens of thousands of positions and close plants in Germany.

“We are planning to bring our ⁠biggest and most premium SUVs, and produce them here in Macon, Georgia,” Döllner said at the rally in Perry near Macon, in a highly unusual move for a European executive during a hard-fought US electoral campaign.
He called the plans, which foresee factory construction starting next year and car production beginning in the 2030s, “a long-term investment because we believe in the American market”.

Audi is the only premium car manufacturer without its own factory in the US, making it particularly vulnerable to Trump’s punishing 15% import tariffs, which cost it an estimated €1.2bn last year. The Macon plant would build 200,000 SUVs annually.

The head of the powerful German trade union IG Metall, Christiane Benner, called Döllner’s US appearance “extremely embarrassing, politically unacceptable and unworthy of the company, but above all of Audi’s employees”.
She accused Döllner of being in “flagrant breach” of the company’s code of conduct, “which expressly requires political neutrality in the run-up to elections”.
She warned that any major investment like the Macon plant would have to go before VW’s supervisory board. Benner is the board’s deputy chair.
after newsletter promotion

Volkswagen is locked in a battle between management and labour over a push to cut as many as 100,000 jobs and close factories. It has blamed the downsizing on intense competition from Chinese carmakers, as well as US tariffs and the expensive transition to electric vehicles.

Its German ​factories are under particular pressure to drive down costs, with Audi’s facility in Neckarsulm, which employs 15,000 people, among four VW plants threatened with closure from early next decade.
“Each site must do its part in terms of competitiveness and the long-term strength of Audi,” a company spokesperson said.

Trump is deeply unpopular in Germany and has riled its political mainstream by vocally backing the far-right Alternative für Deutschland. The AfD is the country’s most popular party, according to polls, and has actively courted Trump’s support.

The 3 November election in Georgia could be decisive in the Democrats’ battle to regain a majority in the Senate. The incumbent senator, Jon Ossoff, is fighting a tough re-election battle against Republican challenger Mike Collins, in a state Trump won in 2024.
Trump has argued ahead of the midterms that his tariffs on car imports are helping the US economy.

articles.title: Celebrations in Serbia after veteran ruler Vučić loses election to student-led protest movement
articles.summary: The populist right-wing leader of 12 years says it is "clear" his party has lost the vote billed as a referendum on the country's future.
articles.byline: André Rhoden-Paul, Jaroslav Lukiv, Paul Kirby

blocks.text: Celebrations in Serbia after veteran ruler Vučić loses election to student-led protest movement
Watch: Joy and disbelief on Serbian streets as Vučić concedes election defeat
ByAndré Rhoden-PaulJaroslav Lukiv and Paul KirbyEurope digital editor
Serbia's long-standing leader Aleksandar Vučić has admitted defeat to a student-led protest movement in snap parliamentary elections.
Celebrations erupted as crowds descended on the centre of Belgrade, Novi Sad and other cities.

The student movement was formed less than two years ago in response to a railway station disaster blamed on corruption and negligence, but fought the election with candidates from a cross-section of Serbian society.

"It is clear we have lost these elections," right-wing populist leader Vučić said as he conceded. With 97% of polling stations counted, Serbia's election commission said the students had won 2.25 million votes and the former ruling party 1.67 million.
The students had secured 52.7% of the vote, while Vučić's Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) was on 39.2%, according to its preliminary figures late on Monday morning.

Vučić had spent two terms as president and could not seek a third term, so was leading his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister, which he left in 2017.
He called the snap elections after two years of protests triggered by the collapse of a canopy in front of Novi Sad station which killed 16 people.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Vučić said early results made it "clear" that his party had lost

blocks.text: Image source, EPA/Shutterstock
Vučić said early results made it "clear" that his party had lost
The Student List's lead candidate Ilija Srdanović told BBC Serbian: "This will be a free state."
He said the anti-corruption movement, which had attracted anti-government voters across Serbia, hoped to "free the country from tyranny".
There were celebrations on the streets of the city, with people dancing and chanting "victory", cars honking, and fireworks set off. "Serbia is free," one student told the BBC. "It's a miracle."

During a celebration speech, Student List candidate Radomir Saicic said Serbians had shown "no obstacle was greater than their will", Reuters reported. "No force can forever overpower a people who have decided to take their destiny into their own hands," he added.
Amid scenes of people dancing in the streets Belgrade, Selena Lebovic said the result was "really fabulous".
"We are all crying, and what to say. We couldn't believe that it would be so easy," she told Reuters.

blocks.caption: Image caption, An aerial photo shows the size of the celebrations by Students' List supporters at  Slavija square in Belgrade

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
An aerial photo shows the size of the celebrations by Students' List supporters at Slavija square in Belgrade
Vučić made his announcement at the headquarters of his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) in the capital Belgrade.
The centre of Novi Sad - the northern city that triggered the student-led protests - was crowded. "Everything is going to get better now," David Vasić, one of those celebrating, told BBC Serbian.
The Student List - which has no obvious leaders and whose members are not used to politics - had attracted anti-government voters across Serbia.
It decided to field candidates to the 250-member parliament from across Serbian society including doctors, actors, academics and sports personalities.

"This is not an ordinary election victory, this is an avalanche that has wiped out an authoritarian regime and entire political scene," said Nebojša Vladisavljević, professor of political science at the University of Belgrade.
There were now two big political groups in Serbia, and the Student List had "absolute legitimacy" to govern for the coming years, he told BBC Serbian.

The anti-corruption movement campaigned on a manifesto that included purging officials who broke rules cracking down on protesters, stopping party loyalists from leading public enterprises, and freeing the public broadcaster of political control.
Vučić and the SNS party have repeatedly denied corruption.

Vučić, who backed Serbia's candidacy for the European Union while refusing to impose sanctions on Russia over its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, had pledged to increase pensions and public sector salaries, and investment in state healthcare.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov praised Vučić's contribution to relations with Russia and hoped "the new political force" in Belgrade would understand that co-operation with Moscow was in Serbia's interests: "But, as you know, it takes two to tango."

His defeat was welcomed by Hungary's prime minister, Péter Magyar, who said he was delighted to hear from the Student List's leaders "how much strength our victory in April had given them". Magyar's party ended 16 years of Viktor Orbán rule, while Vučić's SNS party had been in power since 2012.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ilija Srdanović, Student List's leading candidate, pictured during celebrations late on Sunday

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Ilija Srdanović, Student List's leading candidate, pictured during celebrations late on Sunday
European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos said "a new chapter can begin for Serbia. The door to the EU is open, and we are ready to move forward together".
Earlier in the day, long queues were seen outside polling stations in cities and towns across Serbia.
This was also the case outside booths in a number of countries with sizeable Serbian communities - including Slovenia's capital Ljubljana, Germany's Munich, and Los Angeles and Chicago in the US.
In France, Serbian voters waited in line in heavy rain in Paris.
The election was held amid high tensions across Serbia, with police sealing off streets around the Republic Electoral Commission (RIK) in Belgrade.

Attention will now turn to who will lead the Student List as prime minister. Presidential elections are due to take place in December, with parliament speaker Ana Brnabić currently filling the role in a caretaker capacity.

articles.title: Nurse killed in attack while responding to Ebola alert in DR Congo
articles.summary: Local youths reportedly accused the health workers of contaminating water sources and spreading Ebola.
articles.byline: Basillioh Rukanga, Emery Makumeno, Makuochi Okafor

blocks.text: A nurse has been killed and another health worker seriously injured in an attack as they were responding to an Ebola alert in north-eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

The two were targeted by local youths who accused them of contaminating water sources and spreading the Ebola virus, according to the UN-backed Radio Okapi. The World Health Organization (WHO) condemned the attack.
In an attempt to prevent the virus spreading, neighbouring Uganda has banned all non-essential travel to and from DR Congo and says its citizens returning from there will be quarantined for 21 days.
More than 4,800 people have died and nearly 10,000 been infected in DR Congo since this outbreak began in May.

Reacting to the attack in DR Congo, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said health workers "must be able to carry out their duties in safety and dignity", adding that healthcare personnel should always be protected.
The UN agency also extended its condolences to the family and colleagues of the nurse who was killed and wished the injured worker a swift recovery.
The BBC has contacted the Ebola response team for comment on the circumstances surrounding the attack in DR Congo.

This is not the first time such an attack has happened in DR Congo. Last month, a politician was beaten to death after promoting measures to stop the spread of Ebola, while in August, the Red Cross said its volunteers had been injured and an ambulance set on fire in 11 violent incidents during the first 100 days after the outbreak was declared.
Earlier this month, two countries - Kenya and Nigeria - reported their first cases of Ebola linked to the current outbreak.
The patient in Nigeria was on Monday flown from Abuja to Switzerland for further treatment.

She is the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat who had travelled to the Ugandan capital for a holiday, according to the head of Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention Jean Kaseya. She was evacuated alongside her husband, who has shown no symptoms.
Nigeria's health ministry said she was stable, conscious and able to communicate.
Authorities are now trying to establish where she contracted the virus.

The new restrictions announced in Uganda come after questions were raised over her case and that of a Kenyan businessman. Both tested positive for Ebola after travelling through Uganda, even though no cases have been reported there since August.
The Kenyan had arrived from DR Congo where he had business interests.

Only essential travellers, including aid workers, truck drivers and security personnel, will be allowed to cross the border from DR Congo to Uganda, subject to strict health screening, the health ministry announced.
In addition, all travellers entering Uganda, regardless of their country of origin, will be required to complete locator forms to facilitate contact tracing where necessary.
It said returning Ugandans would "undergo 21 days of quarantine at their own cost".
About 60 people who were being monitored after coming into contact with the Kenyan patient have all been discharged, it added.
In Kenya, the first group of 20 contacts of the first case have gone home, after spending 21 days in quarantine, the health ministry announced on Monday.
Another 98 are still being supervised, while seven people who have tested positive for Ebola were stable it said.
The Kenyan businessman died two days after arriving in Nairobi. A second woman, related to the businessman, died over the weekend.
"All these are measures to ensure that we keep Uganda free of Ebola," Uganda's Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi told the BBC's Newsday programme.

Since the two cases were reported in Kenya and Nigeria this month, Uganda has repeatedly stressed that no cases have been reported within its borders. Uganda recorded 20 Ebola cases and two people died shortly after the outbreak started in DR Congo, but the World Health Organization declared the country free of the disease in August.
The two passengers tested positive after passing through Uganda's Entebbe airport on the same day.
Diana Atwine, the health ministry's permanent secretary, said CCTV camera footage showed no physical interaction between the two patients.

Ugandan officials had previously said the patient in Nigeria had travelled to eastern DR Congo, only transiting through Uganda. On Sunday, however, the health ministry said Uganda and Nigeria were both working to establish her movements, complete travel history and possible routes of exposure.
The Ugandan health minister said the recent cases meant the risk had not ended and further underscored the need to "remain vigilant".
"We share a border with [DR Congo], where transmission continues, and our communities remain closely connected through trade, travel and family ties," Baryomunsi said.
The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
The Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind this outbreak is relatively rare and there is still no vaccine or specific treatment - though trials are under way.
Additional reporting by Swaibu Ibrahim in Kampala

articles.title: Chris Brown given suspended eight-month prison sentence over nightclub attack
articles.summary: The R&B star previously pleaded guilty to affray, after attacking a music producer with a glass bottle.

blocks.text: US singer Chris Brown has avoided jail after striking a man twice in the head with a glass tequila bottle in a London nightclub.
The R&B star was given an eight-month prison sentence, suspended for 12 months, over the attack at private members' club Tape in Mayfair, in the early hours of 19 February 2023.

Brown's vocal coach, rapper Omololu Akinlolu, who joined the attack, was sentenced to four months' imprisonment, suspended for 12 months. Both men, who had pleaded guilty to affray, were also ordered to pay £1,500 costs.
Judge Tony Baumgartner said Brown's use of the glass bottle to hit the victim twice over the head "was plainly dangerous", adding that the violence of the attack was "intense".
The sentence means Brown will not be imprisoned unless he commits another offence during the 12-month period of suspension.
The court heard Brown's attack on music producer Abraham 'Abe' Diaw left the victim in need of hospital treatment for his injuries.

In sentencing, Judge Baumgartner said: "The repeated use of a glass bottle in that way, especially aimed at the head, was plainly dangerous, it carried the risk of delivering a more serious injury than was ultimately sustained."
CCTV footage was shown where Brown struck Diaw four times with the bottle, connecting twice with his head, and then hitting his shoulder.
Sentencing Brown, Judge Baumgartner said: "This was not planned violence. It was nevertheless serious violence by two people in a crowded nightclub."
The judge told Brown: "Violence of this kind in a crowded nightclub is serious, it creates an obvious risk, not only to the person against whom it is directed, but also to others nearby."
He added that Brown's conduct was "particularly dangerous" and that he had to be "physically pulled away" from the attack.
The judge said Brown's fame, commercial success and professional standing "do not entitle you to special treatment - the law applies equally to everyone".

But judge Baumgartner also said he had noted Brown's guilty plea, compliance with bail conditions, and the impact a custodial sentence would have on Brown's children, and said the singer's "risk of further offending is low".
Brown and Akinlolu pleaded guilty to a charge of affray at Southwark Crown Court in July.
The singer had been due to face a trial on more serious charges, which he denied, and which were subsequently dropped.
These were assault, attempting to cause grievous bodily harm, and having an offensive weapon.

Following Brown and Akinlolu's guilty pleas, the CPS released a statement outlining that Brown had approached Diaw on the dance floor, hitting him over the head with a glass bottle twice, before Akinlolu then punched Diaw in the head.
"They continued their assault whilst the victim attempted to flee through the club," the CPS said. "The victim was kicked while he was seated defenceless on the floor."

Judge Baumgartner told the pair that while he had concluded they had both crossed the threshold to be jailed, this year's changes to sentencing laws meant that he had to put off doing so, unless there were exceptional reasons.

"I have considered whether the seriousness of the offending, taken together with the need for punishment and deterrence, amounts to exceptional circumstances requiring immediate imprisonment. I have concluded, in relation to each of you, that it does not," he said.
"These were serious offences deserving of custodial sentences, but the circumstances do not justify displacing the [new legal] requirement that those sentences be suspended."
On Monday, the court was shown three pieces of CCTV footage from inside Tape nightclub on the night of the attack.
The attack lasted no more than 20 seconds, but Brown could be seen hitting the victim four times with a tequila bottle, twice to the head.
Prosecutor, Heidi Stonecliffe KC, described the weapon as a "heavy square-shaped tequila bottle" and said Diaw was approached by Brown at around 03:00.
The footage showed that the nightclub was very small and packed at the time.
The defence described Chris Brown as a "dedicated and a loving father of four children," someone who is "positive and present".
The singer is described as having lived "a good and law-abiding life" since his last conviction in 2013.
The events in Tape nightclub were described by the defence as a "short and deeply regretted incident".
Brown's defence lawyer told the court that he apologises to all those present at the club at the time of the attack.
"This is an ugly and unattractive incident," Sallie Bennett-Jenkins KC said.
"It is, however, an incident which was very short-lived, lasting something more than 17 seconds but no more than 20.
"It is something which undoubtedly would have caused distress to those who are present and for which Mr Brown... offers a profound apology to all those present."
The court heard Akinlolu "genuinely believed" that Brown was "under attack" when he joined the attack, punching Diaw.
Brown was described as being like a "brother" to Akinlolu, his lawyer Laurie-Anne Power KC told the court.
She added: "He genuinely believed him to be under attack and became involved, and thereafter accepts his initial involvement very quickly evolved into the events he has pleaded guilty to."
Diaw was taken to St Mary's Hospital in London after the attack. Ms Stonecliffe KC said he was discharged with "pain relief and a diagnosis of head injury and superficial injury of the knee".
An MRI scan taken in early March showed a "high grade injury to a ligament on the inner side of the left knee", the court heard.
Defending Brown, Ms Bennett-Jenkins KC said there was a "relatively low level of force" and disputed how significant the injuries were.
The defence argued that the attack left no fractures or broken skin and there was an absence of serious injuries.
Diaw, the victim, was "not supportive of the prosecution" and "withdrew" his support some time after the incident, the court heard.
Brown and Akinlolu stood up and faced one another and clasped hands after the judge concluded his sentencing remarks before walking out of the glass dock.
There were loud cheers outside the court as Chris Brown left the building as he appeared to stop to sign an autograph.
After the sentencing, Brown shared a video from inside his car on his Instagram story, showing him looking out the window before turning to the camera and giving a thumbs-up.

Affray is an offence under the Public Order Act and a person is deemed guilty in law if they use or threaten "unlawful violence towards another" with their behaviour, leading someone to fear for their personal safety.
Brown, 37, is considered one of the biggest stars in R&B, with a string of hit songs including Turn Up The Music, Ayo, Freaky Friday, Run It, Forever, Yeah 3x and Don't Wake Me Up.

articles.title: US Marine indicted for murder and robbery of woman in Japan
articles.summary: Prosecutors have indicted Devin Jacob Ballard for a killing that has caused outrage in Japan, local media reports.

blocks.text: A US Marine has been indicted on suspicion of murdering and robbing a woman in Japan earlier this month in a case that has triggered protests, Japanese media reports.
Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, who was stationed at US Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, was arrested on suspicion of killing Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in Naha, the capital of Okinawa.
Prosecutors have now indicted him for allegedly strangling Yagi with a telephone cord and then stealing her backpack and wallet on 3 October, media reports, citing the indictment document.
It wasreported Ballard had denied the allegations, but Asahi Shimbun and Kyodo News cited investigators saying he has made some statements suggesting involvement.
Security footage allegedly shows a man believed to be the suspect entering the hotel with the woman and leaving alone with her belongings.
Yagi's death has caused outrage in Japan, with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi describing the crime as "brutal and heinous".

Earlier this month, the Marine Corps said it was "actively cooperating with Japanese authorities, in response to allegations of serious criminal actions by a Marine" and extended condolences to the victim's family.
It is the latest case involving a US serviceman in Okinawa, which hosts the highest concentration of around 55,000 US soldiers stationed in Japan.

Previous criminal cases have sparked anger and protests, the largest of which took place in 1995, when tens of thousands took to the streets following the abduction, beating and rape of a 12-year-old girl.

In 2024 alone, there were four sexual assault cases involving US troops in Okinawa, including that of air force member Brennon Washington, who was given five years for the rape and kidnapping of an underage girl.
In 2025, US marine Lance Cpl Jamel Clayton was sentenced to seven years in prison for sexually assaulting a woman.
Okinawa Governor Genta Koja said the prefecture has repeatedly demanded that the US take action to prevent such incidents, and said he sees the alleged crime as a sign of a lack of discipline.

The prime minister said her government has registered a "strong" protest with the US and called for "strict disciplinary action against US military personnel and thorough measures to prevent a recurrence of such incidents".

People in Japan have been voicing anger, with some 100 people protesting in both Naha and Tokyo earlier this month. Others took to social media expressing their outrage and demanding justice, with one user saying: "Enough is enough."

articles.title: Macron vows 'strong measures' to combat protests that rocked France
articles.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron said his government will announce "strong measures" in response to violent protests in France in recent weeks. But he also acknowledged that students have…

image.caption: President Macron visited Marseille city hall which was vandalized during recent protestsImage: Aurelien Morissard/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The French government is set to announce a series of "strong measures" to assuage protests which have rocked France in recent weeks, President Emmanuel Macron said on Monday.

Speaking in the southern city of Marseille, Macron warned that fresh demonstrations planned for this coming Saturday were "risky" and said that protest routes would remain outside city centers in order to protect public order.
France braces for 'lively' Halloween
French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told broadcaster BFM that he was expecting further disturbances on October 31.
"Halloween evening is traditionally always a bit lively," he said. "We expect it to be complicated again."

Prior to Macron's arrival in Marseille, the Elysee Palace said the president intended to "pay tribute to and thank the internal security forces that helped restore republican order" in France's second-largest city where protesters briefly stormed the city hall on October 17.

He acknowledged that French authorities had "not anticipated at all" the scale of demonstrations which descended into widespread violence in looting in several major cities, leading to suggestions the state had lost control of the streets.
Macron: 'Social media is damaging our democracies'

The French president also highlighted the role of social media in the protests, saying the online networks were "damaging our democracies" by "bringing young and not-so-young people to places where criminal acts, attacks and looting were taking place."
He described social media as "tools for mobilizing the worst impulses."
France protests continue despite police crackdown

While Macron admitted that French security forces underestimated the extent to which "extreme left forces" would meet up "so early in the day" on October 17, Interior Minister Nunez highlighted the phenomenon of organized far-right mobs confronting left-wing activists in several cities.
"We ​knew there had been calls from numerous identity-based and nationalist movements to come out to defend businesses," he told BFM.
"In a number of cities, such as Nice and Montpellier, these groups arrived in organized formations, mainly to target the ultra-left movement."
A presidential aide said Macron wanted to demonstrate that "the state is present, standing firm and fulfilling its mission to protect."

The president said that curfews enabled relative order to be maintained during last Saturday's protests (October 24), when authorities also deployed 70,000 police officers across the country, making 1,435 arrests.
"The state prevailed this weekend. The state was strong," government spokeswoman Maud Bregeon told RTL radio.
France: Macron acknowledges 'legitimate' student demands

Nevertheless, President Macron also said he had instructed his government, led by Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, to "respond to the legitimate demands that lie at the root of this social movement."

He said the government will soon announce several "concrete and huge" measures aimed at addressing student concerns over education and university admissions, following a nationwide consultation with high school and university student representatives.
France: Why students are taking to the streets
"There are demands that must be heard and answered," confirmed government spokeswoman Bregeon.
"But to answer them, ​there is a prerequisite: a return to calm. We cannot have a functioning social dialogue in a climate of violence such as the one we experienced a week ago."

articles.title: Japanese prosecutors charge US marine suspected of robbing and killing woman
articles.summary:
Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, denies charges that he fatally strangled Anna Yagi, 39, in a hotel on the island of Okinawa

Prosecutors in

blocks.text: Prosecutors in Japan have filed formal charges against a US marine suspected of murdering and robbing a woman while stationed on the country’s island of Okinawa, according to Japanese media.

Devin Jacob Ballard, a 20-year-old lance corporal assigned to Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Okinawa, is charged with fatally strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in the city and stealing from her a backpack containing a wallet, the public broadcaster NHK reported.

Ballard had initially been arrested in Yagi’s killing on 4 October, about a day after she was found dead in Naha, Okinawa’s capital. Prosecutors indicted him in the case on Sunday, and he has reportedly denied the charges.

NHK and other Japanese media outlets had previously reported that Ballard was arrested after surveillance camera footage from near the scene of Yagi’s killing showed a man entering a room with a woman and later leaving the scene with her belongings.
Ballard evidently matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage, was confronted and agreed to accompany investigators voluntarily to a local police station, Japanese media reported.

While being questioned by police, Ballard denied having a hand in Yagi’s killing, saying, “I don’t know anything about it,” NHK reported. But during subsequent questioning Ballard was alleged to have “made statements that partially hinted at his involvement”, the broadcaster reported.
A statement reported by NHK and reported to Yagi’s family on Sunday expressed a hope that Ballard “will confront what he has done and make amends commensurate with what he has done”.
“She lost her life at the young age of 39,” the statement from Yagi’s family added. “She … wanted to live much, much longer.”

Yagi’s killing prompted protests in Okinawa and the Japanese capital of Tokyo, with political leaders publicly condemning her killing. It also triggered a curfew and alcohol ban for US military members stationed in Okinawa, where most of the 54,000 US troops in Japan are based.
Crimes committed by US troops in Japan – including rape, assault, hit-and-run and drunk-driving – have long strained relations between the countries, which are close military allies.
A Japanese court in June 2025 sentenced US marine Jamel Clayton, then 22, to seven years in prison after he was convicted of choking and sexually assaulting a woman in her 20s.
In 2017, a former US marine and civilian military base worker named Kenneth Shinzato was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local Okinawa woman.
US military forces in Japan that same year banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated US marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing a local driver, age 61.
The Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper reported that about 6,000 US military personnel have been arrested since the US returned Okinawa to Japan after the second world war in 1972.
There were 80 such arrests in 2024, constituting a 20-year high.

After Ballard’s arrest, Shinjiro Koizumi, Japan’s defense minister, said: “Incidents and accidents involving US military personnel cause great anxiety among the local community and must not be allowed to happen.”
Reuters and Agence France-Presse contributed reporting

articles.title: Germany's Merz heads to Asia as security issues loom large
articles.summary: Chancellor Friedrich Merz will be meeting the leaders of Singapore, Japan and South Korea as Germany seeks to adjust its foreign policy to rising uncertainty and threats to global supply chains.

image.caption: Merz's visit to Asia will be his longest foreign trip since he took office in May 2025Image: Kay Nietfeld/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz kicked off a five-day tour of Asia on Monday, traveling to Singapore before his scheduled visits to Japan and South Korea. Merz is accompanied by an entourage of 30 senior businesspeople, including representatives of Germany's industry, tech and defense companies, and energy suppliers.
At the same time, Germany's President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is visiting China.
While the trips are not officially related, they both seem aimed at boosting Berlin's economic and security relationships at a time of geopolitical instability, which threatens global supply chains.
Japan needs close allies

In Singapore, Merz is set to deliver a major foreign policy speech and meet Prime Minister Lawrence Wong. He will then travel to Japan on Wednesday to meet with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and take part in the German-Japanese Business Summit.
Merz's visit "will be very much welcomed in Tokyo," said Ben Ascione, an assistant professor of politics and international relations at Tokyo's Waseda University.
"For more than a decade, Japan has been looking to generate new security allies and closer trade partnerships," he told DW.
Will Japan become the Indo-Pacific's most trusted power?

"This greater outreach was started under Prime Minister [Shinzo] Abe, but Takaichi is very much following that blueprint because of the growing tensions in the Indo-Pacific region and the greater uncertainty around the second administration of [US President] Donald Trump," he added.
Germany and Japan face different, but connected threats

The challenges posed by an increasingly expansionist China in the region are of deep concern to Tokyo, particularly as Beijing is forging closer ties with both Russia and the unpredictable regime in North Korea. China and Russia have conducted joint military exercises off Japan, and Beijing is resolute in its insistence that Taiwan be brought under the control of the mainland.

Ascione points out that any conflict over Taiwan, the disputed islands of the South China Sea or territorial claims elsewhere in the region would have a major impact on global trade. Such disruptions would also impact Germany.
How Japan, South Korea and Taiwan hedge vs. US shifts

"Japan and Germany have different primary security threats at the moment, with Germany focused on the Russian invasion of Ukraine and Japan keeping a close watch on China, North Korea and Russia, but I do believe that Germany has come more into line with Takaichi's perception of the security threat that is posed by China," Ascione said.

"Takaichi is going to underline the importance of a rules-based order and the policy of a free and open Indo-Pacific at a time of such geopolitical uncertainty," he added. "Japan has in recent years moved towards greater resilience building, supply chain resilience and more and deeper security partnerships."
German military assets welcome in Japan

According to Ascione, Japan would also "welcome" Germany deploying its military assets to the region, following its Bayern frigate docking in Tokyo in 2021 and its fighter jets conducting air drills with Japanese fighters in 2024.

The frigate Bayern became the first German Navy warship to dock in Tokyo in 20 years in May 2021 and went on to conduct air and maritime exercises with Japanese units. In July 2024, German Eurofighter Typhoon aircraft similarly carried out air drills with Japanese fighters over northern Japan.
Merz and Takaichi are expected to exchange views on responding to geopolitical threats.
Pacifist Japan is rearming — this is why

This would include ensuring supply chain resilience, protecting strategically important industries and ensuring access to technologies and components, such as the rare earths that are critical to a range of advanced technologies but remain largely controlled by China.
European nations 'irritated' by Seoul's outreach to North Korea

Merz is then scheduled to visit South Korea, where he will meet with President Lee Jae-myung and open the 19th Asia-Pacific Conference of German Business in Seoul. He is also due to visit the Demilitarized Zone that marks the border between North and South Korea.
Security issues will again dominate discussions in Seoul, believes Saeme Kim, a research fellow at The Asan Institute for Policy Studies.
However, the German leader could voice concerns about South Korea's perceived "outreach" efforts towards North Korea and, by extension, Russia.
"There has been discussion recently about exports of petroleum to Russia, although Seoul says it has not breached sanctions," she said.
Why Seoul wants an apology from Zelenskyy
South Korea is trying to set up a way to communicate with Pyongyang, according to the expert, despite the regime of Kim Jong Un sending troops to the conflict in Ukraine.
"It's not just Germany, I think a lot of European countries will be irritated by the Lee administration trying to improve relations with North Korea and Russia," Kim said.
The South also continues to provide humanitarian assistance to North Korea, even as the regime forges ever closer economic ties with China and Russia.
"The government needs to keep in mind that some of these policies are going to be damaging to South Korea's own interests over the long-run," she said.
Can South Korea learn from Germany's history?
At the same time, Merz could also offer insight into two Koreas trying to work with one another, drawing on the German experience of reuniting in 1990.

"There are lessons that South Korea can learn, of course, but there are a lot of differences," Kim said. "The two Koreas are still technically at war and Seoul has to deal with an aspiring nuclear power on its border."

Merz will have the opportunity to see the North at a distance when he visits the DMZ. His visit to the border, however, could also be canceled due to lingering tensions over the North Korean mine injuring three South Korean soldiers last month. Pyongyang has accused the South of staging the incident.

articles.title: Steinmeier in China: A major state visit in uncertain times
articles.summary: President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is traveling to China on a state visit in a period of political and economic uncertainty. Germany is seeking alternative partners in the region, but also wants good…

image.caption: Steinmeier begins a five-day trip to China on MondayImage: Hendrik Schmidt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Eight years have passed since Frank-Walter Steinmeier's last trip to China. Since then, the relationship between China and Europe has changed significantly. The German president plans to spend several days touring China before concluding his visit in Beijing, where he will meet with China's leaders.
His visit comes just as the Chinese Communist Party's Central Committee is convening for its plenary session, a major annual event that foreign dignitaries usually avoid when timing their visits.

The focus of the president's five-day trip will be "Germany's diverse and complex relations with China, as well as the challenges involved," his office said in a statement. In addition to sites of cultural exchange, the itinerary will also include a visit to a Volkswagen plant in Hefei.
A diplomatic balancing act

The automotive industry, in particular, illustrates the dilemma facing Germany's China policy. China is one of the most important markets for German automotive and machinery manufacturers, as well as for the chemical industry. At the same time, state-supported overcapacity in China is putting pressure on European manufacturers.
Not only that. Germany and Europe are dependent on China for raw materials and technologies, which means they are increasingly seeking out alternative partnerships.

Steinmeier was once an advocate of the policy of "change through trade" — the idea that other countries could be persuaded to become more democratic with the leverage of global trade — which has few adherents left in Germany today.

Now he must now pursue a tougher European line in Beijing. Caught between partnership and competition, Europe leaders recently managed to reach an agreement: Imports of plug-in hybrid vehicles from China are to be scaled back.
"That was a concrete step, but it can only be the beginning," said Michael Laha, an expert on China at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP) in Berlin.
Why big automakers are losing China
Chancellor and president both in Asia

Coinciding with Steinmeier's state visit to China, Chancellor Friedrich Merz is traveling to the Indo-Pacific with business representatives. His visit to Japan, Singapore and South Korea will focus on competitiveness, technological upheavals, defense cooperation and critical raw materials. Merz is visiting companies and attending important regional economic conferences in Tokyo and Seoul.

The dual trips are Berlin's attempt to send a twofold message: While the chancellor is "deliberately strengthening Germany's partnerships in the Indo-Pacific at a time of global upheaval," according to Laha, the president is seeking dialogue with Beijing at a time when Germany and Europe are recalibrating their relationship with China.

"This joint trip sends a very well-coordinated message to the Chinese that we remain committed to the partnership but at the same time are taking steps to reduce risk," said Laha, before adding that this is a difficult balancing act that also allows China to save face.

blocks.caption: Steinmeier and Merz are traveling to Asia at the same timeImage: Markus Schreiber/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Little room for human rights

While Merz will be accompanied by a large economic delegation, Steinmeier will be traveling to China with representatives from German culture, politics, and academia. Mikko Huotari, director of the China Institute MERICS, is also expected to be part of the delegation — even though Beijing has imposed sanctions on the institute. "The fact that he is coming along sends a clear message to the Chinese side that we do not approve of the sanctions," said Laha.

In 2021, the EU imposed sanctions against several Chinese party and regional officials, as well as an organization accused of serious human rights violations and oppressing the Uyghur minority. It was the first time such sanctions had been imposed on China since the Tiananmen Square massacre in 1989, and Beijing did not take kindly to them:
. In response, the Chinese government imposed entry bans and other sanctions against European politicians, scholars, and institutions, including MERICS.

Laha did not expect human rights to play a major role in the German president's trip. Steinmeier is considered a pragmatist when it comes to China policy. As foreign minister, he distanced himself from his predecessor Joschka Fischer, a critic of China, and even criticized Chancellor Angela Merkel when she hosted the Dalai Lama.

blocks.caption: China's Xi Jinping is seeking greater influence in international affairsImage: Florence Lo/Reuters/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: China should assume international responsibility

On the subject of Ukraine, Steinmeier is likely to be more direct and raise the issue of China's role in the conflict. "Beijing is clearly on Moscow's side," said Laha. In Berlin, however, officials are convinced that China can do more to persuade Russia to engage in serious negotiations and find a solution to the conflict.

Steinmeier may make this clear in his speech at Peking University on Thursday. Germany has "long viewed China's emergence with respect and goodwill," read a statement from the president's office. Today, however, the focus is less on China's continued rise and more on how it uses its growing power.

"If the president points out that Russia used its power to attack a sovereign state, he could be alluding to another regional connection: Taiwan," said Laha. That could be seen as an appeal to Beijing to assume more responsibility for the regional and international order.

To conclude his visit, Steinmeier will meet with China's leadership in Beijing. Talks are planned with President Xi Jinping, whom he has known for nearly two decades, as well as with Premier Li Qiang and the chairman of the National People's Congress, Zhao Leji.

The trip marks the culmination of Steinmeier's focus on Asia during his second term in office. Since then, he has deliberately sought to forge close ties with partners in the region and has advocated for greater diversification. Now China – Germany's most important and most challenging partner – will come to its own conclusion.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Canada's Eric Bauza, modern voice of Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and others, dead at 46
articles.summary: Eric Bauza of Scarborough, Ont., the Emmy-award winning voice actor best known for the iconic Bugs Bunny, has died.

blocks.text: Toronto
Eric Bauza of Scarborough, Ont., the Emmy-award winning voice actor best known for the iconic Bugs Bunny, has died.
Emmy-award winning voice actor's family said he passed away 'suddenly' in an Instagram post
Canadian voice actor Eric Bauza, who portrayed Looney Tunes characters, dead at 46
Eric Bauza of Scarborough, Ont., the Emmy-award winning voice actor best known for the iconic Bugs Bunny, has died. He was 46.
Bauza's family announced he had passed away "suddenly" in a post to his Instagram profile Sunday night. The family did not say the cause of death, but indicated they would share more at a later time.
A report by the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner says Bauza died at his home of hypertensive cardiovascular disease.

Bauza, who was known as a modern successor to original Bugs Bunny voice actor Mel Blanc, grew up watching Bugs Bunny's cartoon exploits at his home in Ontario. In 2020, he was charged with bringing the character to life in all his carrot-munching, prank-pulling glory for HBO Max's Looney Tunes Cartoons, which ran for six seasons.
"It is a dream come true," Bauza told host Ismaila Alfa on CBC Radio's Metro Morning at the time.

In addition to Bugs Bunny, Bauza voiced multiple other characters including Daffy Duck, Tweety Bird and Marvin the Martian. It took two auditions and plenty of practice to land the parts, he told Alfa.
Canadian behind the voice of Bugs Bunny
In 2020, he gave his advice to young voice actors, telling them to remember that, at its base, it's "about the acting, first."
"You have to instill a performance that's grounded in reality," he said.
Among Bauza's credits are such TV shows as The Looney Tunes Show, SpongeBob SquarePants and Bob's Burgers.
He also voiced Foghorn Leghorn, Road Runner, and others in this year's Coyote vs. Acme movie.
Bauza was a regular on the convention circuit, and spoke on a panel at Lightbox Expo in Pasadena, Calif., the day before he died.
Tributes pour in
Jerry Beck, an animation historian, moderated that panel and wrote about it on the website Animation Scoop after Bauza's death.

"He was vibrant and alive," Beck wrote. "To demonstrate a classic piece of Looney Tunes comedy he performed as Bugs Bunny doing the square dance call from 'Hillbilly Hare', while the classic cartoon ran on a large screen beside us, to a packed room full of hopeful artists, cartoonists and budding voice over performers."

Bauza was a "unique voice talent," who brought joy and laughter to millions around the world, Warner Bros. Television Group and US Networks chair Channing Dungey and Warner Bros. Pictures Animation president and chief creative officer Bill Damaschke said in a post on Instagram Monday.

"Eric was a treasured part of our animation family. Our hearts go out to his loved ones," the two said. "Eric said that carrying on the legendary legacy of the Looney Tunes was among the greatest honors of his life."
In an online tribute, fellow voice actor Josh Keaton said Bauza was a gifted and humble performer, and remembered him for having a warm smile and always being sincere.
"He let his talent speak for itself and made everyone feel like he was their biggest fan," Keaton said on social media.
"He will always be a legend but I'm devastated that I'll never be able to give him a hug, or hear him joke or see him smile again."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Gabriela Silva Ponte has been with CBC Toronto since January 2025. Currently, she works as a web writer, but has previously taken on a variety of reporting roles in ethnic media newsrooms and at Toronto Metropolitan University. Gabriela graduated from TMU with a Bachelor of Journalism. You can reach her at gabriela.silva.ponte@cbc.ca.
With files from Kate McGillivray and The Canadian Press

articles.title: Most polls now closed in GTA with election results coming soon

image.caption: The health club of the Allenway condo building in Ward 8 Eglinton-Lawrence is one of the 11 places where voting times have been extended. (Haydn Watters/CBC)

blocks.text: GTA votes: Election night 2026

Who will lead Toronto and across the Greater Toronto Area? Watch CBC Toronto’s live election night special, starting at 7 p.m. ET on Oct. 26, for real-time results, expert analysis and on-the-ground reporting. We’re tracking the biggest mayoral battles and key Toronto city council races.

items: October 27Pool and politicsThe health club of the Allenway condo building in Ward 8 Eglinton-Lawrence is one of the 11 places where voting times have been extended. (Haydn Watters/CBC)Hello, I'm Haydn Watters and I'm a reporter with CBC Toronto’s Metro Morning radio show. Tonight, I’m going to be roaming the city speaking to new winners — those candidates who have never been elected to city council before. I don’t know exactly where I’m headed yet, so we're passing time at the health club of the Allenway condo building in Ward 8, Eglinton-Lawrence. It’s one of the 11 places where voting times have been extended. (This one was kept open until 8:10.)

Premier Ford 'ready to work' with tonight's winnersOlivia PierceyDid Ford hint at endorsing Olivia Chow for Mayor? Here’s what he said'The mayor and I have a phenomenal relationship,' said Premier Doug Ford Wednesday, alluding to a potential endorsement of Olivia Chow for mayor. CBC’s Shawn Jeffords breaks down what was said.Shortly after most polls closed, Ontario Premier Doug Ford made a post on X thanking candidates for putting themselves forward to serve the public. "Our government is ready to work with everyone who is elected tonight on the issues that matter most to Ontario families," Ford wrote. While Ford has not endorsed a candidate to be Toronto’s next mayor, his influence has loomed large in the municipal race. At one unrelated news conference in September, he appeared to all but endorse Chow, but he later walked it back, saying his statements were not an endorsement of the current mayor’s bid for re-election.

Caledon extends voting hours to 10 p.m.Isha BhargavaThe Town of Caledon has just announced it is extending voting hours until 10 p.m. at all voting locations due to what officials are calling "increased volume." We're checking what exactly that means and will report back.

Breaking down Pickering mayoral hopeful Lisa Robinson's controversial recordRochelle RaveendranControversial Pickering councillor Lisa Robinson is running against incumbent mayor Kevin Ashe. Since 2023, she’s been investigated nine times by the city's integrity commissioner for her conduct. (City of Pickering)Lisa Robinson is one of the most divisive figures on Pickering council. She’s running against incumbent mayor Kevin Ashe, with a long record of conduct complaints and pay suspensions behind her. The city's integrity commissioner has investigated Robinson's conduct nine times since 2023. She’s received multiple pay suspensions ranging from 30 to 90 days. The most recent investigation from June focused on comments Robinson made about residential schools. While the commissioner said they couldn’t ban what they called "residential school denialism," they recommended a 90-day pay suspension over comments the councillor made that were found to disrespect city staff. Robinson and Ashe have also repeatedly found themselves at odds. Back in January 2025, Ashe moved council meetings online, citing safety concerns he linked to Robinson’s supporters. That same month, CBC News reported that Ontario Provincial Police were investigating a criminal harassment complaint filed by Ashe on behalf of council. But police told CBC News the investigation ended in March 2026, with no evidence to support criminal charges.

When did Mississauga's race shift to a 3-way battle?Arrthy ThayaparanThis summer, polls and media coverage in Mississauga mainly centred on a Crombie versus Parrish mayoral race, said CBC panellist David Valentin. But once September hit, he said, Tedjo started making "big bold policy proposals" that led to a shift in support in the polls.The race's shift into a three-way battle was "super charged" after mayoral debates were held, Valentin said.

Crombie supporters confident she can win her old job backNav NanwaBonnie Crombie's supporters are starting to arrive at her election headquarters in Mississauga. Many have said they feel confident the city's former mayor will be elected to her old job once again. (Nav Nanwa/CBC)Hi everyone, I'm Nav Nanwa, host of CBC News Peel. I am coming to you from Bonnie Crombie's headquarters in Mississauga, right by Pearson airport. People are starting to file in, but it still feels a little early. Crombie is expected to arrive around 8 p.m. Regardless, people are enjoying some coffee, tea, Indian sweets like gulab jamun and periodically we're hearing soothing jazz music when the election feeds aren't on. The team members we've spoken to so far feel confident that tonight will be her night.

Most polls now closing in TorontoAlina SnisarenkoPolls across the city are now closing, and the vote counts will soon start trickling in. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)Good evening, I'm Alina Snisarenko, a digital reporter at CBC's Toronto newsroom. Polls across the city are now closing, and the vote counts will soon start trickling in. If you are in line at a polling station, stay there. You should still be able to cast your vote.There are also some polling stations that have extended their hours past the 8 p.m. closing time. The following locations have delayed closing times "due to disruptions earlier in the day," per a city news release: Ward 11, Wigwamen Terrace closes at 8:05 p.m.Ward 7, Driftwood Public School closes at 8:08 p.m. Ward 11, Casa 2 closes at 8:08 p.m.Ward 11 & 13, St. Joseph's College closes at 8:08 p.m. Ward 8, The Allenway closes at 8:10 p.m. Ward 11, Aura at College Park closes at 8:15 p.m.Ward 13, The Selby closes at 8:17 p.m.Ward 16, Valley Park Middle School closes at 8:18 p.m.Ward 2, Chartwell Scarlet Heights Retirement Residence closes at 8:20 p.m.Ward 5, Country Club Towers A closes at 8:20 p.m.Eligible voters can only cast their ballot in the ward they live in.You can catch the live count for the mayoral votes here.

October 26Supporters begin arriving at Carolyn Parrish’s election night partyJayden DillI'm Jayden Dill with CBC Peel, reporting from the Le Treport Wedding & Convention Centre, where current mayor Carolyn Parrish is holding her campaign party.The party hasn't started yet, but Parrish supporters are slowly trickling into the sounds of disco music and the smell of pork, roast beef and turkey sandwiches, among other hors d’oeuvres.Venue staff told us they're expecting hundreds of people, having laid out 200 chairs with plenty of standing room.Peter McCallion, son of the late Hazel McCallion, just arrived in his classic all-black suit and cowboy hat. Peter released a video supporting Parrish and blasting Crombie, saying his mother began regretting supporting former mayor Bonnie Crombie before she passed.

Brampton, Mississauga both saw high turnout for advance votingIsha BhargavaMore than 44,000 voters in Mississauga cast their ballots early, setting what the city calls "a new mark for advance voting turnout." It’s a 57 per cent increase from advance voting in the 2022 municipal election, the city said. Brampton boasted a similar increase. Nearly 25,000 Bramptonians cast their ballots during advance voting last week, according to the city — an estimated eight per cent increase compared to the previous municipal election. Historically, Peel Region has had one the lowest voter turnouts in an Ontario municipal election. In 2022, just under 22 per cent of Mississauga residents voted. That same year, the turnout in Brampton was also low with 24.56 per cent votes. Both cities were below the provincial average of 33 per cent.

When did we see a shift in Toronto’s mayoral polls?Arrthy ThayaparanPollsters have been covering the election campaign since January, said David Valentin, a CBC panellist and principal at Liaison Strategies. For a long time Bradford struggled to gain a foothold in the polls, he said on CBC Toronto's election special. But he got a boost in support after former mayor John Tory decided not to run, Chris Alexander withdrew from the race and he began debating Chow."It's always so hard going against an incumbent," Valentin said.

articles.title: Who is Lula? From ex-worker and prisoner to Brazil's president again
articles.summary: The firebrand left-winger, who has at times been at odds with Trump, has won his fourth term as Brazil's president.

blocks.text: Lula's first presidential victory in 2002 marked the end of an unprecedented journey from poverty.
The son of a poor, illiterate peasant family, Lula worked as a peanut seller and shoe-shine boy as a child, only learning to read when he was 10 years old.
He went on to train as a metalworker and found work in an industrial city near São Paulo, where he lost the little finger of his left hand in an accident in the 1960s.
Lula was not initially interested in politics, but threw himself into trade union activism.

Elected leader of the 100,000-strong Metalworkers' Union in 1975, he transformed trade union activism in Brazil by turning what had mostly been government-friendly organisations into a powerful independent movement.

In 1980, Lula brought together a combination of trade unionists, intellectuals, Trotskyites and Church activists to found the Workers' Party (PT), the first major socialist party in the country's history.
The PT went on to gradually replace its revolutionary commitment to changing the power structure in Brazil with a more pragmatic, social democratic platform.
Lula came to power promising major reforms to the country's political and economic system.
He vowed to eradicate hunger and create a self-confident, caring, outward-looking nation.
In his time in office, Lula pumped billions of dollars into social programmes and can reasonably claim to have helped reverse Brazil's historic inequalities.

By increasing the minimum wage well above the rate of inflation and broadening state help to the most impoverished with a family grant programme, the Bolsa Familia, he helped some 44 million people and cemented his support among the poor.
However, many commentators argue that the programme failed to address the structural problems that underpin poverty, such as a lack of education.

He left office eight years later, after serving two terms as president, enjoying exceptionally high popularity ratings for a retiring Latin American leader - 83% - having raised Brazil's profile on the international scene and presided over the longest period of economic growth in three decades.

Unable to run for a third term, Lula left the presidency and, shortly afterwards, was diagnosed with throat cancer. He even shaved his trademark beard during treatment. Doctors declared him cured of the disease in 2012.

Under his chosen successor, progress stalled. The economic boom also gave way to recession, and the country's political scene was rocked by a huge investigation into top-level corruption, known as Operation Car Wash.

Lula was among those to get caught up in the scandal. In July 2017, he was convicted of corruption and sentenced to more than nine years in prison for accepting a beachside flat as a bribe from engineering firm OAS - a sentence increased on appeal to 12 years.

Lula was also jailed for 12 years and 11 months for corruption and money laundering for receiving bribes from two construction and engineering firms by way of funding improvements in a country house he and his family used.
He has always maintained his innocence, insisting accusations against him were politically motivated.
In 2019, he was released after having served just over 18 months, after a Supreme Court ruling that the incarceration had been illegal, having come before all appeals had been exhausted.
Those convictions were annulled in 2021, leaving Lula free to run for a third term in 2022, beating right-winger Jair Bolsonaro.
When he re-entered office in 2023, he vowed it would be his last term, and yet his party endorsed him as their candidate again this year, even though he will turn 81 on Tuesday.
Even backers of the PT will acknowledge that he achieved more in his first two terms - from January 2003 to December 2010 - than in his most recent four years in office.

And while his supporters described him ahead of the 2022 election as the "saviour of the Amazon", praising his commitment to protecting the rainforest, some environmentalists have been critical of some of his recent actions.
His support for exploratory oil drilling in offshore waters near the mouth of the Amazon in particular has drawn criticism.
Lula insists that he remains committed to eventually phasing out fossil fuels and argues that oil revenues are key to financing Brazil's transition to clean energy.

His government has also pointed to the reduction in deforestation in the Amazon - satellite data suggests the area deforested in the first half of 2026 was reduced to its lowest in the past decade - as proof that its policies were working.
Lula's third term coincided with the return to office of Trump.
The two men represent different ends of the political spectrum and have found it impossible not to voice their differences in public.
The Brazilian leader told the BBC in September 2025 that he had no relationship with Trump.

Even though the US has a trade surplus with Brazil, Donald Trump imposed 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods in July that year, citing the trial on coup charges of Brazil's right-wing former president Jair Bolsonaro as a trigger. Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year jail sentence and it was his son, Flávio, who Lula beat in Sunday's election run-off.

Lula accused Trump of foreign interference and said "he's not emperor of the world". But their relationship improved after a White House in May this year, after which the two leaders exchanged public compliments - Trump called Lula "dynamic", while the Brazilian president said he left the meeting "very satisfied".
In July of this year, the US imposed 25% tariffs on most goods, external from Brazil.
The two governments still disagree on key issues such as crime, and Lula acknowledged they are especially far apart on trade.

Referring to what Trump has dubbed the "Donroe doctrine" - his administration's national security strategy which asserts that US dominance in the Western hemisphere should not be interfered with - Lula has insisted that "Brazil does not fit into anyone's backyard".
